teile.einleitung: Taurine is a substance that does important jobs in the bodies of people and animals, for example in the heart, in the eyes and in digestion. For cats it is especially important, because their bodies can hardly make it themselves. They therefore have to take it in with animal food such as meat or fish.
wichtigste: Taurine is a substance similar to an amino acid that is found in animal tissue.
Cats can hardly make taurine themselves and need it from animal food.
If cats lack taurine, they can go blind and develop a heart disease.
Taurine is almost never found in plants.
The name comes from the Latin word “taurus” for bull.
Dogs and humans can make taurine themselves.

abschnitte.text: **Taurine** is a small chemical building block that resembles the amino acids, but is not used to build proteins. It is found in almost all animal tissues, especially in the heart muscle, in the retina and in the brain. It was discovered in 1827 in the **bile** of cattle. That is where the name comes from, because “taurus” is the Latin word for bull.

Taurine helps with the **digestion of fat**, because in the liver it combines with bile acids. It is important for the healthy beating of the heart muscle. In the **retina** it protects the light-sensitive sense cells. It also helps the cells to keep their balance of water and salt.

Cats are pure **meat eaters**, and their bodies have adjusted to the fact that taurine is in every meal. That is why they can make it themselves only in very small amounts. They also need a lot of it, because they make their bile acids only with taurine. A mouse or a piece of meat supplies enough, but an entirely plant-based diet does not.

abschnitte.titel: Consequences of a lack of taurine
abschnitte.text: In the 1970s and 1980s many domestic cats became ill because their ready-made food contained too little taurine. They developed a disease of the retina that can lead to **blindness**. Others suffered from a dangerous weakness of the heart in which the heart muscle widens. Since this became known, taurine has been added to cat food, and the diseases have become much rarer.

Cats should be given proper **cat food** and not dog food all the time. Dog food often contains too little taurine, because dogs can make it themselves. A vegetarian or vegan diet is also dangerous for cats without supplements. When cooking with a lot of water, part of the taurine is lost, which is why food with added taurine is safer.

begriffe.erklaerung: A small building block from which the body builds proteins.
A fluid from the liver that helps with the digestion of fat.
An animal that feeds mainly on other animals.
The layer in the eye with the sense cells for sight.

gewusst: Taurine is also added to energy drinks, although a healthy person makes enough of it themselves.
The taurine in energy drinks and cat food is made in the laboratory today and is not obtained from bulls.
Mussels, squid and fish are among the foods with especially much taurine.

teile.einleitung: The ostrich is the largest and heaviest bird in the world. It cannot fly, but it runs faster than a racehorse. It lives in the savannahs and semi-deserts of Africa.
wichtigste: The ostrich belongs to the running birds, the so-called ratites.
Its genus is called Struthio, and the name Struthio camelus means roughly “camel sparrow”.
Besides the common ostrich, the Somali ostrich is today usually regarded as a species of its own.
An ostrich has only two toes on each foot.
In a sprint it reaches about 70 kilometres per hour.
Its eye is about 5 centimetres across and is therefore bigger than its brain.
The common ostrich is regarded as not endangered, the Somali ostrich as endangered.

abschnitte.text: A male ostrich can grow to about 2.5 metres tall and weigh over 100 kilograms. The male has black feathers with white wing and tail feathers, and the female is greyish brown. The neck and legs are long and almost bare. The eyes have a diameter of about **5 centimetres**, which are the biggest eyes of all land animals. Each foot has only **two toes**, and the bigger one carries a strong claw.

Ostriches are the fastest of the running birds. In a sprint they reach about 70 kilometres per hour and can run at around 50 kilometres per hour for a long time. A single stride at full speed can be 3 to 5 metres long. They use their small **wings** for steering and braking. With powerful kicks they can even defend themselves against lions.

The **common ostrich** lives in savannahs and semi-deserts in large parts of Africa. The **Somali ostrich** lives in the Horn of Africa, and in the males the skin on the neck and thighs is blue-grey. In the past a subspecies also lived on the Arabian Peninsula. This Arabian ostrich was wiped out, and the last known wild one died around 1966.

Ostriches eat mainly plants, seeds, leaves and flowers. Sometimes they also eat insects, lizards and other small animals. They swallow small stones, which help to grind up the food in the **stomach**. For a long time they can manage without drinking, because they take in water from plants.

The male scrapes a shallow hollow in the sand. In it the main hen and often other females lay their eggs. An ostrich egg weighs about 1.5 kilograms and is the largest bird’s egg in the world. During the day the well-camouflaged female usually sits on the eggs, at night the black male. After about six weeks the chicks hatch.

The common ostrich is classed as not endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature, **IUCN**, while the Somali ostrich is classed as endangered. Ostriches are threatened by hunting and the loss of their habitat. Ostriches are kept on farms for their meat, feathers and leather. There are also some ostrich farms in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: Large birds that cannot fly and get about by running, for example the ostrich and the emu.
A group of closely related species, called Struthio in the ostrich.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature, which records in the Red List how badly species are threatened.
A list that shows which species of animals and plants are threatened.

gewusst: The eye of an ostrich is bigger than its brain.
The idea that ostriches stick their head in the sand when in danger is a myth, and at most they lie flat on the ground.
A single ostrich egg is roughly equal to 20 to 25 hens’ eggs.

teile.einleitung: Camouflage means that an animal looks in such a way that it hardly stands out in its surroundings. Some animals have the colour of their background, others look like a twig, a leaf or a stone. In this way they protect themselves from enemies or creep up unnoticed on their prey.
wichtigste: Camouflage helps animals not to be seen.
When an animal looks like an object or another living thing so as not to be noticed, it is called camouflage.
Many fish have a dark back and a light belly, which camouflages them from enemies and prey.
The mountain hare and the rock ptarmigan change their colour to white in winter.
Stick insects look like dry twigs.
Chameleons and cuttlefish can change their colour in a short time.
Hunters such as leopards or tigers also use camouflage to creep up on prey.

abschnitte.text: The simplest form of camouflage is a colouring like the background, called **cryptic colouration**. The brown hare is earth brown like a field, the tree frog green like a leaf. In the Swiss Alps the **mountain hare**, the rock ptarmigan and the stoat wear a white coat in winter and a brown one in summer. The colour change is triggered mainly by the length of the day.

In **mimesis**, an animal resembles an object or an uninteresting living thing. Stick insects look like twigs, leaf insects like leaves with veins and signs of gnawing. The caterpillars of some geometer moths keep still and stick out at an angle from the branch like a little twig. Some moths sit on bark and blend almost completely into it.

Many fish, dolphins and penguins have a dark back and a light belly, which is called **countershading**. Seen from above, the dark back blends with the dark water in the depths. Seen from below, the light belly matches the bright surface of the water. In this way the animals are equally hard to see for enemies and prey.

Spots and stripes break up the outline of a body, which experts call **disruptive colouration**. A leopard in the leaves or a tiger in tall grass is therefore hardly to be seen. In zebras the stripes probably make it harder for predators to follow a single animal in the herd. Roe deer fawns, too, are well camouflaged with their white dots in the light and shade of the forest floor.

Some animals can actively change their colour: **chameleons**, cuttlefish and flatfish such as the flounder adapt in seconds to minutes. They have special colour cells in the skin for this. A distinction is made between camouflage and **mimicry**: in this a harmless animal imitates a dangerous one, like a hoverfly with wasp stripes. People, too, have copied camouflage from animals, for example in camouflage suits and camouflage nets.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal adapts to its surroundings in colour or shape so as not to stand out.
Camouflage by resembling an object, for example a twig or a leaf.
A dark back and a light belly, as in many fish.
A harmless animal looks like a dangerous one in order to scare off enemies.

gewusst: The cuttlefish can change not only its colour but even the surface of its skin, so that it looks like stone or algae.
Because there is often less snow at lower altitudes in winter, white mountain hares there sometimes stand out especially.
Polar bears have black skin under their light-looking fur and are still perfectly camouflaged in the snow.

teile.einleitung: The Sumatran elephant is a subspecies of the Asian elephant that lives only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra. It is somewhat smaller and lighter than other Asian elephants. Sadly it is critically endangered, because its rainforest keeps getting smaller.
wichtigste: The Sumatran elephant is a subspecies of the Asian elephant.
It lives only on the island of Sumatra in Indonesia, in South-East Asia.
It is somewhat smaller than other Asian elephants.
It lives in rainforests and eats large amounts of plants.
The herds are led by an experienced matriarch.
It is regarded as critically endangered.
The greatest danger is the clearing of the rainforest for plantations.

abschnitte.text: Sumatran elephants grow to about 2 to 3 metres tall and weigh several tonnes. They have somewhat lighter skin and fewer pigment patches than other Asian elephants. Like all **Asian elephants**, they have smaller ears than African elephants and two bumps on the forehead. The tip of the trunk has only one finger-like projection. Only the males have **tusks**, and these are often rather short.

The Sumatran elephant lives only on the island of **Sumatra**, which belongs to Indonesia. It inhabits tropical rainforests in the lowlands and in hilly areas. Sumatra is the sixth-largest island in the world. The Sumatran tiger, the Sumatran rhinoceros and the orangutan also live on the island.

Elephants are pure **plant eaters**. They eat grasses, leaves, bark, roots and fruit. A grown elephant eats up to 150 kilograms a day and drinks a great deal of water. In doing so they spread many plant seeds in the forest in their droppings.

Females and young live in family groups led by an old **matriarch**. Adult males usually live alone or in small bachelor groups. An elephant cow is pregnant for about 22 months, as long as no other land mammal. The young one is protected by the whole herd for years.

Since 2011 the International Union for Conservation of Nature has classed the Sumatran elephant as **critically endangered**. Large parts of its forest have been cleared for oil palm and paper wood plantations. When elephants raid fields, conflicts with farmers arise. Estimates give only about 1000 to 2000 animals, as of around 2020. In Way Kambas National Park and in other protected areas, people are trying to protect the last herds.

In Switzerland you can see Asian elephants, for example, at Zurich Zoo. There, since 2014, is the large **Kaeng Krachan Elephant Park**. Zoos work together in breeding programmes to keep healthy populations. With donations they also support the protection of wild elephants in Asia.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group within an animal species that lives in a particular area and differs a little.
The experienced older elephant cow who leads the herd.
A very large planting on which only one crop is grown, for example oil palms.
Lengthened front teeth of elephants, made of ivory.

gewusst: Elephants are pregnant for almost two years, longer than any other land mammal.
In Way Kambas National Park, tamed elephants and their keepers help to keep wild elephants away from fields.

teile.einleitung: The Sumatran rhinoceros is the smallest and most primitive species of rhinoceros in the world. It is the only rhinoceros that still has a reddish-brown coat of hair, and it is the closest living relative of the extinct woolly rhinoceros. Today it is one of the rarest large mammals on Earth.
wichtigste: The Sumatran rhinoceros is the smallest species of rhinoceros.
It is the only rhinoceros that still has some fur on its skin.
It has two horns on its nose.
It lives in rainforests on Sumatra and Borneo.
It is a loner and likes to wallow in mud.
Its closest relative was the extinct woolly rhinoceros.
It is critically endangered, and there are probably fewer than 80 animals.

abschnitte.text: With a shoulder height of about 1 to 1.5 metres, the Sumatran rhinoceros is the smallest rhinoceros. It weighs about 500 to 1000 kilograms. Its skin is reddish brown and covered with **hair**, which is especially dense in young animals. It has two horns, and the front one is longer. Its scientific name is Dicerorhinus sumatrensis.

The Sumatran rhinoceros lives in dense tropical **rainforests** in hills and mountains. In the past it was found from India and Myanmar through Thailand and Malaysia to Sumatra and Borneo. Today there are only small groups left on Sumatra and in the Indonesian part of Borneo. In Malaysia it has been extinct since 2019.

The Sumatran rhinoceros eats leaves, twigs, young shoots and fruit. It usually lives alone and is active mainly early in the morning and in the evening. During the day it often rolls for hours in a muddy **wallow**. The mud cools the skin and protects against insects.

abschnitte.titel: A relative from the Ice Age
abschnitte.text: The Sumatran rhinoceros is the oldest rhinoceros group still alive. Its closest relative was the **woolly rhinoceros**, which in the Ice Age also lived in Europe and in the area of present-day Switzerland. The woolly rhinoceros died out over 10 000 years ago. The hairy coat of the Sumatran rhinoceros still recalls this relative.

The Sumatran rhinoceros is regarded as **critically endangered**. Experts estimate that fewer than 80 animals are still alive, scattered in small groups. Poachers hunt rhinoceroses for their horn, which in some countries is wrongly believed to be a medicine. In addition their forest is being cleared, and the few animals hardly find any partners.

In **Way Kambas National Park** on Sumatra there is a protection centre in which Sumatran rhinoceroses are bred. In 2001 the first Sumatran rhinoceros for over 100 years was born in human care at Cincinnati Zoo in the USA. It was called Andalas and today lives in Way Kambas, where it has had young of its own. Every birth is an important success for this species.

begriffe.erklaerung: An extinct rhinoceros with thick fur that lived in Europe and Asia in the Ice Age.
The illegal hunting of protected animals.
A muddy puddle in which animals roll about.
An animal that usually lives alone.

gewusst: The Sumatran rhinoceros is more closely related to the woolly rhinoceros of the Ice Age than to the rhinoceroses in Africa.
A rhinoceros horn is made of keratin, the same material as our fingernails.

teile.einleitung: A vet is a doctor for animals. If a dog is ill or has to be vaccinated, you go to them. Vets look after pets, farm animals, horses and even zoo animals.
wichtigste: Sick animals are taken to the vet.
Vets vaccinate, examine, operate and advise animal owners.
There are specialists for small animals, horses, farm animals and zoo animals.
In Switzerland you study veterinary medicine at the Vetsuisse Faculty in Bern or Zurich.
Vets also check foods such as meat and milk.
The first veterinary school in the world was founded in Lyon in 1761.

abschnitte.text: Vets examine sick and injured animals and treat them with medicines or an **operation**. They vaccinate animals against dangerous diseases such as rabies or feline distemper. They put a **microchip** into dogs and cats and can neuter animals. They also advise on how to feed and keep an animal properly.

A **small animal practice** treats dogs, cats, rabbits, guinea pigs and birds. Farm animal vets drive out to farms and look after cows, pigs, sheep and goats. Horse vets specialise in horses, and zoo vets treat elephants, lions or penguins. In large animal hospitals there are even specialists for eyes, teeth or the heart.

Anyone who wants to become a vet studies **veterinary medicine**. In Switzerland this is possible at the Vetsuisse Faculty, which belongs to the universities of Bern and Zurich. The course lasts five years and ends with a federal examination. After that you can train further in a special field.

Not all vets work in a practice. Every canton has a **cantonal vet**, who, for example, fights animal diseases and oversees animal welfare. Official vets check the meat in slaughterhouses so that it can be eaten safely. At federal level the Federal Food Safety and Veterinary Office, or FSVO for short, is responsible.

Even in ancient times there were people who healed horses and cattle. The first veterinary school in the world was founded by Claude Bourgelat in 1761 in Lyon in France. In Switzerland, veterinary schools were set up in Bern and Zurich at the beginning of the 19th century. Today vet is a very popular job, especially among women.

abschnitte.titel: Tips for a visit to the vet
abschnitte.text: Dogs and cats should go once a year for a check-up and for vaccinations. The best way to carry cats is in a **carrier**. It helps if you write down how long the animal has been ill and what it has eaten. For emergencies at night or at the weekend there is an emergency veterinary service.

begriffe.erklaerung: The science of the health and diseases of animals.
An injection that protects the body against a particular disease.
A vet who oversees animal welfare and animal health for the canton.
An operation after which an animal can no longer have young.

gewusst: A vet has to know the body structure of many different animal species, while a doctor for people needs to know only one.
Zoo vets have to put some animals, such as lions or rhinos, to sleep first with a tranquilliser dart.
The word “veterinary” comes from the Latin “veterinarius”, which means roughly “concerning draught animals”.

teile.einleitung: Echinoderms are sea animals with a spiny or rough skin and a body that is often divided into five parts like a star. They include starfish, sea urchins and sea cucumbers. They live only in the sea, from the shore down to the deep sea.
wichtigste: The starfish is an echinoderm.
Other echinoderms are sea urchins, sea cucumbers, brittle stars and feather stars.
There are about 7000 species alive today.
Adult echinoderms usually have a body with five rays.
Under the skin they have a skeleton made of small plates of chalk.
They move using many small tube feet that are filled with water.
Echinoderms live only in the sea.

abschnitte.text: Echinoderms, called **Echinodermata** in science, form a phylum of their own. Their name comes from the Greek word for “hedgehog skin”. Under their skin lies a skeleton of many small plates of chalk, from which spines or bumps often stick out. Surprisingly, they are more closely related to vertebrates, and so to us, than to snails or insects.

There are five groups alive today: **starfish**, sea urchins, sea cucumbers, brittle stars and feather stars. Starfish usually have five arms, but some species have many more. Sea urchins are round and covered with long spines. Sea cucumbers are long and soft, and brittle stars have thin, very flexible arms.

Echinoderms have a special **water vascular system**, a network of tubes filled with seawater. With it they move hundreds of tiny tube feet that stick out from the underside. With these suction feet they crawl slowly over the seabed and hold on to rocks. Starfish also use them to pull open mussels and eat them.

Many echinoderms can grow lost body parts back, which is called **regeneration**. A starfish that loses an arm grows a new one. In some species, a completely new starfish can even grow from a cut-off arm with a piece of the centre. When in danger, sea cucumbers sometimes push out parts of their insides and grow them again later.

Echinoderms live in all the seas, from shallow tidal pools down to the **deep sea**, where sea cucumbers are often the most common large animals on the seabed. In Switzerland there are no living echinoderms, because they need salt water. In the Jura, however, you can find fossil sea urchins and sea lilies from the time when a sea lay there millions of years ago. Some species, such as sea urchins, are eaten in some countries.

begriffe.erklaerung: The scientific name of the echinoderms.
A system of tubes with seawater that moves the tube feet of echinoderms.
The growing back of lost body parts.
A body that is divided into five equal parts like a star.

gewusst: A starfish has no brain and no blood, but pumps seawater through its body.
Starfish can push their stomach out through their mouth to digest prey outside their body.
The larvae of echinoderms do not have five rays but, like us, a left and a right side of the body.

teile.einleitung: Tracheae are fine breathing tubes in the bodies of insects, myriapods and some arachnids. They carry oxygen straight to the organs, with no lungs at all. Stag beetles, pond skaters and millipedes all breathe in this way.
wichtigste: Tracheae are a branching system of tubes for breathing.
Insects such as the stag beetle breathe with tracheae.
Millipedes also breathe with tracheae.
The air gets in through small breathing openings on the sides of the body.
These openings are called spiracles.
The finest tubes reach as far as individual cells.
Plants also have tracheae, but there they carry water.

abschnitte.text: Tracheae are thin, air-filled **tubes** in the body of arthropods. The word comes from the Greek word for windpipe. Unlike in us, there are no lungs, and the air is spread directly through the whole body. Insects, myriapods and some arachnids breathe in this way.

On the sides of the chest and abdomen there are small holes called **spiracles**. Air flows through them into the tracheae. Many insects can close the spiracles with small flaps so that they do not lose too much water. The pond skater, too, breathes through such breathing openings and tubes.

abschnitte.titel: Like a tree made of tubes
abschnitte.text: From the spiracles the tracheae branch more and more finely, like the branches of a tree. The finest ends are called **tracheoles** and are thinner than a hair. They reach as far as the individual cells, where the oxygen passes in. So that the tubes do not collapse, they are lined with spiral-shaped reinforcements made of **chitin**.

The stag beetle, the largest beetle in central Europe, breathes through tracheae like all beetles. Millipedes have breathing openings on almost every body ring. The great diving beetle in the pond fetches air at the surface of the water and stores it under its wing cases. Mosquito larvae hang from the surface of the water by a small breathing tube.

Plants also have tracheae, but there the word means something different. In plants, tracheae are long, dead tubes of cells in the wood that carry **water** from the roots upwards. They are also called vessels. The similarity lies only in the shape of a long tube.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fine breathing tube in the body of insects and other arthropods.
A small breathing opening on the side of an insect's body.
The finest end of a trachea, which reaches as far as the cells.
A firm substance that the armour of insects is made of.

gewusst: At every moult an insect also sheds the inner skin of its tracheae.
Insects cannot breathe through the mouth, only through the holes on their sides.
If you stuck the spiracles of an insect shut, it would suffocate.

teile.einleitung: Whiskers, which in German are called tactile hairs, are long, stiff hairs with which many mammals feel their surroundings. Best known are the whiskers of cats, which the jaguar also has. With them the animals sense, even in the dark, where obstacles are and whether they can fit through a narrow gap.
wichtigste: Whiskers are called vibrissae in technical language.
They help in feeling the surroundings, especially in the dark.
At their root sit very many nerve cells that report the finest touches.
Cats have whiskers on the muzzle, above the eyes and on the front legs.
Seals sense with their whiskers the water swirls left by swimming fish.
Almost all mammals have whiskers, but humans do not.

abschnitte.text: **Whiskers** or **vibrissae** are thicker, longer and stiffer than ordinary fur hairs. They are set deep in the skin in a sheath that is surrounded by a small blood cushion. There many **nerve fibres** end, which sense even the smallest movements of the hair. The hair itself feels nothing, but works like a lever that passes the touch on to the nerves.

Most whiskers grow on the muzzle and are called **whiskers** there. Cats also have tactile hairs above the eyes, on the cheeks, on the chin and on the back of the front legs. With the hairs on the legs they sense whether the prey between their paws is still wriggling. In many cats the whiskers reach out to the side about as far as the body is wide.

In the dark, a cat can use its whiskers to tell where walls, branches or obstacles are. It even senses **air currents** that arise around objects. When catching prey, it points the hairs forwards to feel the prey from close up, where it cannot see sharply. The **jaguar** and other big cats also use their whiskers when hunting at night.

**Seals** can use their whiskers to sense the water swirls that a fish leaves behind, and so follow it even in murky water. Mice and rats move their whiskers back and forth many times a second and in this way feel out their surroundings. The walrus has hundreds of thick whiskers with which it finds mussels on the seabed. Manatees and beavers also use whiskers.

From the position of the whiskers you can tell a cat’s mood: when it is relaxed they stand loosely to the side, and when it is afraid they lie close to the face. You must never cut off a cat’s whiskers, because it would lose its sense of direction. Now and then a whisker falls out and grows back, and that is normal. Some cats do not like to eat from narrow bowls, because the hairs bump against the edge.

begriffe.erklaerung: The technical word for whiskers.
Tactile hairs on the muzzle, for example in cats and mice.
A fine line that carries signals from the senses to the brain.
Small currents that a swimming animal leaves behind it.

gewusst: A blindfolded seal can follow a fish by its whiskers alone.
In the brain of mice, a small area of its own is responsible for each single whisker.
Some birds, such as nightjars, also have bristle-like feathers at the beak that work like whiskers.

teile.einleitung: A resident bird is a bird that stays in its area all year round and does not fly south in autumn. The great tit, the house sparrow and the great spotted woodpecker are typical resident birds in Switzerland. They have to know some very special tricks to survive the cold winter.
wichtigste: Unlike a migratory bird, a resident bird stays in its area all year round.
Birds such as the great tit, which stay in one place all year, are called resident birds.
Migratory birds such as the swallow fly to warmer countries in autumn.
Partial wanderers roam about the surrounding area in winter without moving far away.
Partial migrants are species in which some of the birds move away and some stay.
In winter, resident birds often feed on seeds, buds and hidden stores.
In Switzerland, many tits, woodpeckers, sparrows and crows are resident birds.

abschnitte.text: Birds have two basic ways of dealing with winter. **Migratory birds** such as barn swallows and swifts fly to warmer countries, often as far as Africa. **Resident birds**, on the other hand, stay in their breeding area all year round. This only works for species that can find enough food even in winter.

There are mixed forms between resident and migratory birds. **Partial wanderers** such as the siskin or the bullfinch roam about in winter and look for areas with more food. In partial migrants such as the blackbird or the robin, some of the birds stay, while others move south. Some mountain birds only move down into the valley in winter.

Typical resident birds in Switzerland are the great tit, blue tit, house sparrow, great spotted woodpecker, jay, nuthatch and carrion crow. There are also resident birds in the Alps, for example the **rock ptarmigan**, the golden eagle and the bearded vulture. In winter the rock ptarmigan has white plumage and digs itself into the snow when it is cold. The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach studies which birds stay and which move away.

Resident birds fluff up their plumage so that a warming layer of air forms between the **feathers**. On cold nights they shiver with their muscles to produce warmth, and look for sheltered places to sleep such as tree holes or nest boxes. Some, such as the nutcracker and the jay, hide thousands of seeds and nuts in autumn as a **store**. In winter they find many of these hiding places again under the snow.

Many people feed birds in winter in the garden or on the balcony. Suitable foods are, for example, sunflower seeds, oat flakes with fat or special bird food, but no bread and nothing salted. The **bird feeder** should be kept clean so that no diseases are passed on. An even more important help is a garden that is close to nature, with native shrubs, berries and seed heads.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird that flies to warmer regions in autumn and returns in spring.
A bird that roams about the wider surroundings in winter.
A bird species in which some animals move away and others stay.
The area in which a bird builds its nest and raises its young.

gewusst: On a cold winter day, a great tit has to eat a large part of its body weight in food to survive the night.
A nutcracker can remember many thousands of hiding places with Swiss pine nuts in winter.
Because of the milder climate, more birds spend the winter in Switzerland today than in the past, for example blackcaps.

teile.einleitung: Mosquitoes, often simply called midges or gnats, are small insects whose females suck blood. Almost every child knows their buzzing at night. In Switzerland their bites are annoying, but mostly not dangerous.
wichtigste: A grown mosquito is only a few millimetres long and has six legs.
On its head it has two large compound eyes.
Only the females bite, because they need blood for their eggs.
A female mosquito lays several hundred eggs at once, mostly on water.
During the day, mosquitoes like to hide in shady, damp places.
Mosquitoes are mostly active in the evening and at night.
In Switzerland a mosquito bite is mostly not dangerous, because hardly any dangerous diseases are passed on here.

abschnitte.text: A mosquito is only a few millimetres long, has six long, thin legs and two narrow wings. On its head are two large **compound eyes**, two antennae and a long, thin piercing proboscis. The males have bushy, feather-like antennae with which they hear the females. There are about 3500 species worldwide, and in Switzerland there are several dozen.

Only the **females** suck blood, because they need the proteins in it to form eggs. Otherwise males and females feed on plant juices and flower nectar. Mosquitoes find us by the carbon dioxide in our breath, our body heat and certain scent substances in sweat. Dark clothing attracts them especially, because they also find their way with their eyes.

The typical **buzzing** comes about because mosquitoes beat their wings up and down several hundred times a second. Males and females buzz at different pitches, and they recognise each other by the sound of their wingbeats. Although the wings beat so fast, a mosquito flies rather slowly. Even a light wind makes flying difficult for it.

The female lays several hundred **eggs** on still water, for example in pools, rain barrels or watering cans. Larvae hatch from them, which live in the water and take in air at the surface through a small breathing tube. After the pupa stage the finished mosquito hatches, and in summer this takes only about one to two weeks. Anyone who covers water containers in the garden or empties them regularly prevents many mosquitoes.

When it bites, the mosquito injects saliva into the skin so that the blood does not clot, and this saliva causes the **itching**. In Switzerland mosquito bites are almost always harmless, because hardly any dangerous diseases are passed on here. In tropical countries, on the other hand, mosquitoes pass on diseases such as **malaria** or dengue, and are therefore among the most dangerous animals in the world. Since 2003 the Asian tiger mosquito has been spreading in Ticino, and by now also north of the Alps, and experts keep watch on it.

begriffe.erklaerung: An eye that is made up of many small single eyes.
A long, thin mouthpart with which the mosquito bites and sucks.
The young form of an insect, which looks different from the grown animal.
An introduced, black and white striped species of mosquito that also bites during the day.

gewusst: When sucking blood, a mosquito can take in more than its own body weight in blood.
Mosquito larvae hang upside down at the surface of the water and breathe through a tube at the rear end.
Bats, swallows and dragonflies eat a great many mosquitoes.

teile.einleitung: Stick insects are insects that look like little twigs or sticks. They belong to the order of phasmids and are masters of camouflage. They include the longest insects in the world.
wichtigste: Stick insects belong to the insect order of phasmids, called Phasmatodea in science.
The name comes from the Greek word “phasma”, which means ghost or apparition.
Unlike true grasshoppers, stick insects cannot jump.
About 3500 species of phasmids have been described.
In 2016 a stick insect of the genus Phryganistria from China, measuring 62.4 centimetres, was presented as the longest insect.
Stick insects eat leaves and are mostly active at night.
In some species, females can have offspring without males.

abschnitte.text: Stick insects have a long, thin body and look like a **twig**. During the day they sit motionless in the bushes and often stretch their front legs forwards so that they look even more like a branch. Some sway gently back and forth like a twig in the wind. In this way they are easily overlooked by birds and other enemies.

Stick insects belong to the order of **phasmids** (Phasmatodea). The name comes from the Greek word “phasma”, which means ghost or apparition, because the animals seem so invisible. The same order also includes the leaf insects, which look like leaves. About 3500 species have been described worldwide, and most of them live in the tropics. They are only distantly related to true grasshoppers and cannot jump either.

In 2008 the species **Phobaeticus chani** from Borneo became known as the longest insect, with a total length of about 56.7 centimetres. Its body without the legs is about 36 centimetres long. It is named after the Malaysian naturalist Datuk Chan Chew Lun. In 2016 a museum in China presented a stick insect of the genus Phryganistria measuring 62.4 centimetres, which beat the record.

The species **Heteropteryx dilatata** from Malaysia is probably the heaviest phasmid, and its females weigh up to about 65 grams. The females are mostly bright light green, the smaller males brown. If the animal is touched, it snaps its thorny hind legs together and can pinch painfully. The female pushes her eggs into the ground one at a time with her egg-laying tube.

abschnitte.titel: Reproduction and keeping them as pets
abschnitte.text: Many stick insects simply let their eggs drop to the ground, where they look like **plant seeds**. In some species, such as the Indian stick insect, eggs also develop without males, which is called parthenogenesis. That is why often only females can be seen in terrariums. Stick insects are popular as pets and in Switzerland they can easily be fed on bramble or ivy leaves.

begriffe.erklaerung: An order of insects that includes stick insects and leaf insects.
When an animal looks so much like its surroundings that it is hardly seen.
Reproduction in which females have offspring without males.
A tube-shaped organ at the rear of the body that some insects use to lay eggs.

gewusst: Some stick insects play dead when in danger and simply let themselves fall to the ground.
If a young stick insect loses a leg, it can grow back during the next moults.
The eggs of some species are carried by ants into their nest, where they are protected from enemies.

teile.einleitung: The tropics are the hot and often very damp belt around the middle of the Earth, on both sides of the equator. Here it is warm all year round, and in many areas it rains almost every day. More animal and plant species live in the tropics than anywhere else, for example gibbons, parrots and jaguars.
wichtigste: The tropics lie between the northern and the southern tropic.
In the tropics it is warm all year round, and there is no cold winter.
Instead of summer and winter there are often rainy seasons and dry seasons.
The tropical rainforests are the habitats richest in species on land.
Gibbons live in the tropics of South East Asia because of the heat and the lots of rain.
Important tropical regions are the Amazon basin, the Congo basin and South East Asia.
Many foods such as bananas, cocoa and coffee grow in the tropics.

abschnitte.text: The tropics lie between the **Tropic of Cancer** in the north and the **Tropic of Capricorn** in the south. Both are about 23.4 degrees from the equator. Between them the sun stands exactly overhead at midday at least once a year. That is why the sunshine is especially strong here.

In the inner tropics near the equator it is damp and hot, often around 25 to 30 degrees. There are often heavy thunderstorms in the afternoon. Further away from the equator, a **rainy season** and a dry season take turns. The days are about 12 hours long all year round, so the difference between day and night is small.

Where it rains a lot, **tropical rainforests** grow, with huge trees in several storeys. The biggest is the Amazon rainforest in South America. Where there is a long dry season, **savannahs** arise with grass and single trees, as in East Africa. Mangrove forests on the coasts are also part of the tropics.

In the tropics live great apes such as orang-utans and gorillas, but also gibbons, which swing skilfully from branch to branch. Colourful birds such as toucans and parrots are typical. Many insects, frogs and snakes live here. Researchers think that more than half of all animal and plant species on Earth are found in tropical rainforests.

Cocoa, coffee, bananas, pineapples and many spices come from the tropics. Swiss chocolate is therefore made from tropical cocoa beans. The rainforests store a lot of **carbon** and are important for the climate of the whole Earth. Sadly, large areas are cleared every year, for example for pastures, soya or palm oil.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imaginary line that divides the Earth into a northern and a southern half.
A line of latitude over which the sun stands overhead at midday on one day of the year.
Months of the year in which it rains especially much.
The number of different animal and plant species in one place.

gewusst: There are even glaciers in the tropics, for example on Kilimanjaro, because the mountains are so high.
Hundreds of species of beetle can live on a single tree in the rainforest.
The word tropics comes from the Greek word for turning.

teile.einleitung: The Sumatran tiger is the smallest tiger still alive in the world. It lives only on the Indonesian island of Sumatra, in rainforests and mountain forests. With its dense, dark stripes it is perfectly adapted to life in the jungle.
wichtigste: The Sumatran tiger is the smallest form of tiger.
It lives only on the island of Sumatra in Indonesia.
Males weigh about 100 to 140 kilograms.
Its stripes are closer together than in other tigers.
It hunts wild boar, deer and other larger animals.
There are only a few hundred Sumatran tigers left in the wild.
It is critically endangered.

abschnitte.text: Male Sumatran tigers weigh about 100 to 140 kilograms, females about 75 to 110 kilograms. That makes them clearly smaller than the Siberian tiger, which can weigh over 250 kilograms. The fur is dark orange, and the black **stripes** lie close together. Males have strikingly long hair on the cheeks and neck, which looks like side whiskers.

The Sumatran tiger lives only on **Sumatra**, the large island west of Borneo. It inhabits lowland rainforests, mountain forests and swamps. Important protected areas are, for example, Kerinci Seblat National Park and Gunung Leuser National Park. Its small size helps it to make its way through dense forest.

The Sumatran tiger is a **predator** and usually hunts alone at dusk or at night. It creeps up on its prey and overpowers it with a pounce. Its prey includes wild boar, sambar deer, muntjacs and tapirs. A tiger needs a large **territory** so that it finds enough prey.

After a pregnancy of about three and a half months, a female usually gives birth to two to three young. The young are blind at first and completely dependent on their mother. They stay with her for about one and a half to two years and learn to hunt in that time. The father does not help to raise them.

The Sumatran tiger is regarded as **critically endangered**. Probably only a few hundred animals are still alive in the wild. The greatest dangers are the clearing of the rainforest for plantations and poaching. Two closely related island tigers, the **Bali tiger** and the Javan tiger, already died out in the 20th century.

Tigers are the largest cats in the world. Today they live only in Asia, from Russia through India to Sumatra. Experts today often group the Sumatran tiger together with the extinct tigers of Java and Bali into one subspecies, the Sunda tiger. In European zoos, Sumatran tigers are kept in a joint **breeding programme**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group within a species that lives in a particular area and has features of its own.
The area in which a tiger lives and hunts and which it defends against other tigers.
The illegal killing of protected animals.
Cooperation between zoos so that a threatened animal species carries on living healthily.

gewusst: No two tiger coats are alike, and the stripes are as unique as a fingerprint.
Tigers like swimming and swim well, unlike many other cats.

teile.einleitung: The striped hyena is a shy hyena with light fur and dark stripes. It lives in North Africa, the Near East and India and is out and about mainly at night. Unlike the better-known spotted hyena, it usually lives alone or in small groups.
wichtigste: The striped hyena has dark stripes on light, grey to beige fur.
It weighs about 25 to 55 kilograms.
It lives in North Africa, the Near East and India.
It eats mainly carrion, but also fruit and small animals.
It is active at night and rests during the day in caves or rock crevices.
When it feels threatened, it raises the mane on its back.
It usually lives alone or in small groups, not in large clans.

abschnitte.text: The striped hyena is about 1 metre long and weighs around 25 to 55 kilograms. Its fur is light grey to beige with **dark stripes** on the body and legs. On its back it has a long **mane**, which it raises when in danger. Then it looks much bigger. Its front legs are longer than its hind legs, so the back slopes downwards towards the rear.

The striped hyena lives in North and East Africa, in the Middle East, in Central Asia and in India. It inhabits dry areas such as savannahs, steppes, semi-deserts and rocky hills. During the day it hides in **caves**, rock crevices or burrows. It needs water within reach.

The striped hyena is mainly a **scavenger**. It eats the leftovers of animals that lions, leopards or tigers have killed. With its extremely strong jaws it can even crack bones. Besides that it eats fruit, insects, eggs and small animals. Near villages it also searches through rubbish.

Striped hyenas are **nocturnal** and often cover long distances in search of food. They usually live alone or in small family groups. They are much quieter than spotted hyenas and hardly ever let the well-known laughing be heard. A female usually has two to four young, which are born blind.

Although hyenas look a little like dogs, they are more closely related to cats, civets and mongooses. There are four species of hyena: the striped hyena, the **spotted hyena**, the brown hyena and the aardwolf. The spotted hyena is the largest species and lives in large clans. The aardwolf eats almost only termites.

The International Union for Conservation of Nature classes the striped hyena as **near threatened**. It is poisoned or hunted because people think it is dangerous or blame it for damage to livestock. The decline of large predators and wild animals also takes food away from it. In some countries it is protected, and it is also kept in zoos.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that eats dead animals that it has not killed itself.
Long hair on the neck or back that an animal can raise.
A large group of animals that live and hunt together, as in the spotted hyena.
An animal that is out and about at night and sleeps during the day.

gewusst: A striped hyena can crack with its teeth bones that would break the teeth of other predators.
Hyenas are more closely related to cats than to dogs.

teile.einleitung: A mare is a grown female horse. After a pregnancy lasting almost a year, she usually gives birth to a single foal. In a herd of horses, experienced mares often play an important part.
wichtigste: A grown female horse is called a mare.
The male horse is called a stallion, and a castrated stallion a gelding.
A young horse is called a foal, and a female foal a filly.
A mare is pregnant for about eleven months.
She usually has only one foal, and twins are very rare.
An experienced lead mare often leads the herd to water and food.
In donkeys and zebras, too, the female is called a mare.

abschnitte.text: Among horses the female is called a **mare** and the male a **stallion**. If a stallion is castrated, he is called a **gelding**. A young horse is called a foal, and a young female horse a filly. From about three to four years old, a female horse counts as a mare.

Mares are ready to mate mainly in spring and summer, and they are said to be **in season**. The season returns about every three weeks. The pregnancy lasts about eleven months. In this way the foals are born the following spring, when there is enough fresh grass.

Usually the mare gives birth to a single foal, often at night. The foal is **precocial** and is already standing on its long, wobbly legs after about an hour. Soon afterwards it drinks the first milk, which contains especially important defence substances. The foal stays with its mother for several months and drinks her milk.

In wild herds of horses there is often an experienced **lead mare**. She decides when the herd moves on and where there is water and food. The stallion guards the herd and drives away strange stallions. On pastures with domestic horses, too, you can watch how a mare leads the group.

In Switzerland many Franches-Montagnes horses are bred, the best-known Swiss breed of horse. At the **National Stud** in Avenches in the canton of Vaud, breeding stallions are kept, while the mares are often kept on farms. In summer many Franches-Montagnes mares live with their foals on the pastures in the Jura. Mares are also used in riding sport and as leisure horses.

In Central Asia people drink fermented mare’s milk, which is called **kumis**. If a mare is mated with a male donkey, the result is a **mule**. Mules are strong and sure-footed and in the past were also used as pack animals in the Swiss mountains. When riding, mares are often just as reliable as geldings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A male horse that has not been castrated.
A castrated male horse, which is usually calmer than a stallion.
The time when a mare is ready to mate.
A young horse in its first year of life.
A cross between a male donkey and a female horse.

gewusst: A foal can run alongside its mother just a few hours after birth.
The pregnancy of a mare lasts almost as long as a whole year.

teile.einleitung: In insects such as bees, wasps and hornets, a sting is a pointed weapon at the rear of the body with which they inject venom. They use it to defend themselves and their nest or to paralyse prey. A sting hurts, but is usually harmless.
wichtigste: Stings are found in hymenopterans such as bees, wasps, hornets, bumblebees and some ants.
The sting is a modified egg-laying tube, which is why only females sting.
The honeybee defends itself with its sting.
The venom of the bee is called bee venom.
The sting of the honeybee has barbs and stays stuck in the skin of mammals.
A honeybee dies after it has stung a person.
Wasps can sting several times because their sting is almost smooth.

abschnitte.text: The sting is a hollow, pointed tube at the end of the **abdomen**. Originally it was an egg-laying tube that females used to lay eggs. In bees and wasps it turned into a venom weapon over the course of evolution. That is why males, the drones, have no sting and cannot sting.

When it stings, the insect presses the sting into the skin and pumps venom into it from a **venom sac**. Bee venom contains several substances that cause pain, redness and swelling. The most important one is called melittin. The venom is meant to drive off attackers who want to plunder the beehive.

The sting of the honeybee has fine **barbs** like a harpoon. If it stings into the elastic skin of a person or another mammal, the sting stays stuck. When the bee flies away, the sting tears out of its body together with the venom sac, and it dies. When the enemy is an insect, however, it can pull the sting out again.

Wasps and hornets have an almost smooth sting and can sting several times. Bumblebees are very peaceful and only sting if you squeeze them or disturb their nest. Some **ants** also have a sting, for example the myrmicine ants. Wood ants, on the other hand, have no sting but spray formic acid.

If a bee sting is stuck in the skin, you should scrape it away quickly, for example with a fingernail. After that, **cooling** with ice or a wet cloth helps against swelling and pain. A sting becomes dangerous if you have an allergy or if it is in the mouth or throat. In that case you must call the emergency number 144 straight away. In Switzerland, a few percent of people have an allergy to bee or wasp venom.

begriffe.erklaerung: An insect group that includes bees, wasps, bumblebees and ants.
Small points that face backwards and stop something from being pulled out.
A small container in which the insect stores its venom.
An oversensitive defence reaction of the body that can be dangerous.

gewusst: A torn-off bee sting keeps pumping venom into the skin, which is why it should be removed quickly.
The queen bee has a smooth sting and uses it mainly against rival queens.
When stinging, a bee gives off a scent that calls other bees to attack and smells a little like banana.

teile.einleitung: Toxoplasmosis is a disease caused by a tiny parasite called Toxoplasma gondii. It can spread through the droppings of infected cats, among other ways, but also through raw meat. For healthy people the disease is mostly harmless, but it can be dangerous for unborn babies.
wichtigste: Toxoplasmosis is caused by the single-celled parasite Toxoplasma gondii.
The parasite spreads through the droppings of infected cats, among other ways.
You can also catch it from raw or undercooked meat.
Cats are the final hosts, in which the parasite completes its life cycle.
In healthy people the disease usually causes no symptoms.
For pregnant women and their unborn child, a first infection can be dangerous.
Washing your hands and well cooked meat protect against infection.

abschnitte.text: Toxoplasmosis is an infectious disease that is caused by the single-celled **parasite** Toxoplasma gondii. The germ can infect almost all warm-blooded animals, that is, mammals and birds, and also people. Worldwide, probably about a third of all people have taken in the germ at some time. Most notice nothing, because the immune system keeps the parasite in check.

Only in cats and other members of the cat family can Toxoplasma complete its life cycle, which is why they are the **final hosts**. Cats usually become infected when they eat infected mice or birds. After that, for a few weeks they pass millions of tiny, tough resting forms, so-called **oocysts**, in their droppings. These become infectious only after one to five days and can survive in soil and sand for months.

People can become infected in several ways. This often happens through raw or undercooked **meat**, for example from pork, mutton or game, in which cysts of the parasite are found. Unwashed vegetables, garden soil or an uncleaned cat litter tray can also pass on germs. A pregnant woman can pass the parasite on to her unborn child through the placenta.

In most healthy people toxoplasmosis causes no symptoms or is like a mild flu with swollen lymph nodes. It is dangerous for people with a weakened **immune system**. If a woman is infected for the first time during pregnancy, the unborn child can be harmed in the eyes or brain. That is why there are special rules of caution for pregnant women.

The parasite was discovered in 1908 in Tunisia by the researchers Charles Nicolle and Louis Manceaux. They found it in a small rodent called a **gundi**, hence the species name gondii. The genus name Toxoplasma comes from the Greek word for a bow, because the germ is slightly curved. Only much later did people find out that cats play a key role in its life cycle.

After contact with cats, soil or raw meat, you should wash your hands thoroughly. It is best to clean the **cat litter tray** every day, because the oocysts become infectious only after a few days. You should cook meat right through and wash vegetables and salad thoroughly. When gardening, gloves protect you.

begriffe.erklaerung: A living thing that lives on or in another and harms it.
The living thing in which a parasite completes its life cycle.
A tough resting form of the parasite that is passed out in the droppings.
The body's own defence against germs.

gewusst: Mice that are infected with Toxoplasma lose their fear of the smell of cats and so are eaten more easily.
Anyone who has had toxoplasmosis once is usually protected from it for the rest of their life.
House cats that live only indoors and are not given raw meat hardly ever become infected.

teile.einleitung: Pond farming means breeding and raising fish in ponds that have been made by people. The most important pond fish in central Europe is the carp, which is often bred in large numbers. The ponds are drained regularly so that the fish can be harvested.
wichtigste: Pond farming is an old form of fish farming in man-made ponds.
Carp are often bred in large numbers in special fish farms.
Many pond areas were laid out by monasteries in the Middle Ages.
In autumn the ponds are drained and the fish are caught.
A table carp needs about three years to grow big enough.
Pond landscapes are valuable habitats for birds, amphibians and insects.

abschnitte.text: In **pond farming**, fish are kept in man-made ponds that can be filled and drained. It is a form of **aquaculture**, that is, the farming of water animals. The ponds are mostly shallow, so that the water warms up quickly and plenty of food grows for the fish. Ditches and sluices allow the water level to be controlled exactly.

The most important pond fish is the **carp**, a peaceful fish that searches the mud for worms, insect larvae and small creatures. It likes warm, still water and tolerates little oxygen. Breeders have developed forms with a few large scales, such as the **mirror carp**. After about three summers a carp weighs around 1.5 to 2 kilograms and is sold as a food fish.

In the Middle Ages it was mainly **monasteries** that laid out large pond systems. On many fast days monks were not allowed to eat meat, but they were allowed fish. That is how the carp spread across the whole of central Europe. Well-known pond landscapes can still be found today in South Bohemia in the Czech Republic, in Lusatia and Franconia in Germany, and in the Waldviertel in Austria.

In autumn the water of a pond is let out slowly until the fish gather in a deep pit in front of the outlet. There the pond farmers take them out with nets and landing nets, which is called **harvesting**. In many regions this is a festival with many spectators. Afterwards the pond is filled again or left dry over the winter so that the soil can recover.

Pond landscapes offer a home to grey herons, ducks, dragonflies, frogs and rare water plants. Besides carp, the ponds are often also home to **tench**, pike and zander. In Switzerland there are only a few carp ponds, although fish ponds were also kept in monasteries in the past. Today it is mainly **trout** and char that are bred here, in farms with cold, flowing water.

begriffe.erklaerung: The farming of fish, mussels or other water animals by people.
Catching the fish when a pond is drained.
A fish that does not hunt other fish.
A bred form of the carp with only a few large scales.

gewusst: In the Czech Republic, Poland and Austria, carp is a traditional Christmas meal.
The largest pond in the Czech Republic, the Rožmberk Pond in South Bohemia, was already laid out in the 16th century.
In the wild, a carp can live for several decades.

teile.einleitung: A trophic cascade is a chain reaction in nature: if the number of an animal at the top of the food chain changes, it has consequences for many other animals and plants further down. The most famous example is the return of wolves to Yellowstone National Park in the USA. There it was clearly shown how whole food webs can change.
wichtigste: Trophic means that it is about feeding and feeding levels.
A cascade is a waterfall in steps, and in the same way the change works from step to step.
Predators at the top, such as wolves, affect plant eaters and so also plants.
In Yellowstone National Park, wolves were brought back in 1995 and 1996.
The wolves hunted elk, and as a result trees such as willows and aspens partly recovered.
Sea otters, sea urchins and kelp forests are also a well-known example.
How strongly a cascade works is still being studied closely by researchers.

abschnitte.text: In nature one animal eats another, which is called a **food chain**. Each step in it is called a **trophic level**: plants, plant eaters, predators. If something changes right at the top, the effect slides downwards like dominoes. This very chain reaction is called a trophic cascade.

In Yellowstone National Park, wolves had been wiped out around 1926. After that the **elk**, a large kind of deer, multiplied very strongly and ate young trees on riverbanks bare. In 1995 and 1996, wolves from Canada were brought back. The elk became fewer and avoided dangerous spots, so that willows and aspens could grow there again.

With more willows on the bank, **beavers** found more food and building material again. Their dams created ponds for fish, frogs and insects. Scavengers such as ravens, eagles and bears benefit from the leftovers of the wolves' prey. The number of coyotes also changed, because wolves pushed them out.

On the Pacific coast of North America, **sea otters** eat sea urchins. Where sea otters are missing, the sea urchins multiply and eat the huge kelp forests of brown algae bare. When the otters return, the kelp forests grow again. These forests offer a habitat to many fish.

Trophic cascades show how important large **predators** can be for healthy habitats. In Switzerland people discuss whether wolves and lynx affect the numbers of roe deer and red deer and so help the forest. Red deer and roe deer like to nibble young little trees. Experts stress, however, that nature is complicated and that not every effect is as clear as in the textbook.

begriffe.erklaerung: Many food chains linked together in one habitat.
A step in the food chain, for example plant eaters.
A predator right at the top of the food chain that has hardly any enemies.
Animals are released again where they had died out in the past.

gewusst: Even the mere fear of wolves changes where deer feed, which is called a landscape of fear.
The beavers in Yellowstone were in part also resettled by people, which makes the research even more exciting.
Fish in lakes can also set off cascades that affect how green the water is.

teile.einleitung: Tapirs are large plant eaters with a short, flexible trunk that live in the forests of Central and South America and South-East Asia. Although they look a little like pigs, they are most closely related to rhinoceroses and horses. They are regarded as “living fossils”, because their build has hardly changed for millions of years.
wichtigste: Tapirs are most closely related to rhinoceroses and horses, and all of them are odd-toed ungulates.
There are four species: the lowland tapir, the mountain tapir, Baird’s tapir and the Malayan tapir.
The name “tapir” comes from the Tupi language of South America.
Tapirs like best to live in damp forests close to water.
They are mostly active at dusk and at night and live as loners.
Young tapirs have a pattern of light stripes and spots for a few months.
Tapirs spread seeds in their droppings and are therefore important gardeners of the forest.

abschnitte.text: Tapirs have a massive body, short legs and a **very short tail**. Their nose and upper lip together form a short, flexible **trunk** with which they grasp leaves. Depending on the species, they grow 150 to 250 centimetres long and weigh over 300 kilograms. Their **skin is thick and tough** and protects them from thorns and branches in the undergrowth.

Like horses and rhinoceroses, tapirs are **odd-toed ungulates**. On the front feet they have four toes, on the hind feet three. Each toe ends in a small hoof, so that they can walk well even on soft, muddy ground. The name “tapir” comes from the **Tupi language**, which was spoken by native people in Brazil.

Three species live in the Americas: the lowland tapir in South America, the mountain tapir in the Andes and Baird’s tapir from Mexico to northern South America. The black and white **Malayan tapir** lives in South-East Asia, for example in Thailand, Malaysia and on Sumatra. All tapirs like **damp forests close to water**. They are excellent swimmers and can even dive, sometimes using the trunk like a snorkel.

Tapirs eat leaves, shoots, fruit and water plants. To take in important **minerals**, they lick at mineral-rich patches of earth, so-called salt licks. They are out and about mainly at **dusk and at night** and usually live as loners. They mark their territory with urine, and with their droppings they spread seeds all through the forest.

A female tapir is pregnant for about 13 months and usually gives birth to only one young. The young one has brown fur with light **stripes and dots**, which recalls a watermelon. This pattern camouflages it in the play of light and shade on the forest floor. After a few months it disappears, and the young animal takes on the colouring of the adults.

All four species of tapir are regarded as endangered or seriously endangered. The main reasons are the **clearing** of the forests and hunting. Because tapirs reproduce slowly, their populations recover only with difficulty. Zoos in Europe take part in breeding programmes to preserve the species.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of mammals with an odd number of toes on the hind foot, including horses, rhinoceroses and tapirs.
A lengthened, flexible nose, in the tapir together with the upper lip.
A spot with mineral-rich earth at which animals lick to take in salts.
An animal that mostly lives alone.
Seeds are carried by animals to new places, where new plants grow.

gewusst: Tapirs in a similar form have existed for many millions of years, and they even lived in Europe in the past.
Tapirs communicate with high whistles that you would hardly expect from such a big animal.
A grown tapir can flee into the water when in danger and walk along the bottom under water.

teile.einleitung: The telescope eye is a bred form of the goldfish with especially large, bulging eyes. They sit at the sides of the head like small telescopes, which is where the name comes from. The fish looks funny, but it needs a lot of consideration and care.
wichtigste: The telescope eye is a bred form of the goldfish.
Typical of it are its large, bulging eyes.
This bred form originally comes from China.
It has a roundish body and a double tail fin.
Telescope eyes swim slowly and see poorly.
Their eyes are easily injured on sharp objects.
It needs a large aquarium with cool, clean water.

abschnitte.text: The telescope eye has a short, egg-shaped body and long, often double fins. Most striking are the **telescope eyes**, which stick out of the head at the sides like small balls. It comes in orange, red, white, spotted and black. The deep black variety is called the “Black Moor” in English.

The **goldfish** is descended from a crucian carp from East Asia and was bred in China more than a thousand years ago. Breeders picked out fish with special features again and again and bred only from these. In this way forms such as the veiltail, the lionhead and the telescope eye came about over time. In Japan the telescope eye is called “Demekin”, which roughly means “goggle-eyed goldfish”.

Young telescope eyes first have quite normal eyes. Only after a few months do the eyes slowly grow outwards. The large eyes are delicate and can be hurt on stones or plants with hard edges. Telescope eyes also do not see especially well and often find their food more slowly than other fish.

Telescope eyes are **coldwater fish** and like water between about 15 and 24 degrees. They need a roomy aquarium with good filtering, because goldfish produce a lot of waste. The furnishings should be soft and without sharp edges. You should not keep them together with quick, greedy fish, because these snatch their food away.

Telescope eyes eat flakes, granules, water fleas, mosquito larvae and also some greens such as peas or lettuce. You should only feed them as much as they eat in a few minutes. With good care they can live to be over ten years old. Like all goldfish, they prefer to live in a small **group** rather than alone.

begriffe.erklaerung: A type of animal that people have created by choosing and breeding on purpose.
A fish that needs cool water without heating.
A popular ornamental fish from East Asia from which many bred forms are descended.
A tail fin that is split into two halves.

gewusst: Telescope eyes are born with normal eyes, and the bulging eyes grow only later.
The black telescope eyes can change colour during their lives and turn bronze or orange.
Because they swim slowly, telescope eyes are not very suitable for a garden pond with fast fish.

teile.einleitung: In some animals it is not the genes that decide whether a male or a female hatches from an egg, but the warmth in the nest. This is called temperature dependent sex determination. It occurs mainly in turtles, crocodiles and some lizards.
wichtigste: In some reptiles the temperature in the nest decides the sex of the young.
In the European pond turtle, the nest temperature decides whether males or females hatch.
In many turtles more females arise when it is warm.
In mammals and birds, on the other hand, the chromosomes decide the sex.
What matters most is usually the middle third of the incubation period.
Climate change can shift the ratio of males to females.

abschnitte.text: In humans, dogs or birds the sex is already settled at fertilisation, because it depends on the **sex chromosomes**. In many reptiles it is different. Here the sex is fixed only during development in the egg. The deciding factor is the **incubation temperature**, that is, how warm the ground around the eggs is.

In most turtles, females hatch from warm eggs and males from cooler eggs. This is also true of the **European pond turtle**. In many species the threshold temperature lies roughly between 28 and 30 degrees Celsius. At exactly this temperature about equal numbers of males and females hatch.

In all crocodiles, too, the sex depends on the temperature. In them, mostly males hatch at medium temperatures and rather females at very cool or very warm ones. In the tuatara from New Zealand it is the other way round from turtles, and there warm eggs give rise rather to males. In some lizards such as the leopard gecko, temperature also plays a part.

The warmth influences certain genes and **hormones** in the embryo. Depending on the temperature, more female or male hormones are made, and the gonads develop into ovaries or testes. A short, sensitive phase in the middle of the incubation period is especially important here. This phenomenon was discovered in 1966 by the French researcher Madeleine Charnier in an African agama lizard.

When beaches and nesting sites get warmer and warmer, almost only females now hatch in many sea turtles. In green turtles in the north of Australia, researchers found that almost all the young animals are female there. Protection programmes therefore sometimes move eggs to shadier places or build shade over the nests. In Switzerland pond turtles are being resettled in a few places, and there too people pay attention to the nest temperature.

begriffe.erklaerung: The process that decides whether a living thing becomes male or female.
Tiny carriers of genetic information in every cell.
The warmth at which the eggs develop.
A living thing at a very early stage of development, for example in the egg.

gewusst: Even a difference of one or two degrees can decide whether a nest produces almost only males or almost only females.
Eggs at the top of the nest are often warmer than those at the bottom, so both sexes can hatch from the same clutch.
In crocodiles, both very cool and very warm nests produce mainly females.

teile.einleitung: A bull is a grown, uncastrated male of the cattle family. He is the father of the calves and is usually clearly bigger and stronger than a cow. Bulls are impressive animals, but you have to be careful when dealing with them.
wichtigste: The male of the cow is called a bull.
A castrated male of the cattle family is called an ox.
Big bulls can weigh over 1000 kilograms.
Bulls are used for breeding cattle.
Many bulls wear a nose ring so that they can be led more easily.
The ancestor of our domestic cattle is the extinct aurochs.
The coat of arms of the canton of Uri shows a bull’s head.

abschnitte.text: Among cattle the female is called a **cow**, the young a **calf** and the grown male a **bull**. If a male is castrated, it is called an **ox**. Oxen are calmer and in the past were harnessed as draught animals in front of carts and ploughs. A young male that is not yet fully grown is called a young bull.

Bulls have a strong neck, broad shoulders and a massive head. Depending on the breed, they weigh about 800 to over 1200 kilograms. That often makes them almost twice as heavy as cows of the same breed. Many breeds have horns, but there are also hornless cattle.

A **breeding bull** is meant to pass on his good qualities to the calves, such as plenty of milk or good meat. Today most cows in Switzerland are no longer covered directly by the bull but by **artificial insemination**. In this way a single bull can become the father of very many calves. Well-known Swiss breeds of cattle are the Brown Swiss, the Simmental and the Eringer.

Bulls can be unpredictable and dangerous, especially when they are protecting their herd. That is why many wear a **nose ring** by which they can be led. On hiking trails through pastures you should keep your distance and not startle the animals. By the way, it is not the colour red that annoys a bull but the movement, because cattle can hardly tell red from green.

All domestic cattle descend from the wild **aurochs**. It once lived in Europe, Asia and North Africa and was much bigger than today’s cattle. The last aurochs died in 1627 in a forest in Poland. People tamed cattle as long as about 10 000 years ago.

The coat of arms of the canton of **Uri** shows the black head of a bull with a nose ring, the so-called Uri bull. The star sign Taurus is also named after this animal. At cattle shows in Switzerland, especially beautiful bulls and cows are given prizes. In some countries there are bullfights, which, however, are controversial and are banned in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A castrated male of the cattle family, which is calmer than a bull.
A young animal of the cattle family in its first year of life.
A method in which the seed of a bull is brought to the cow without mating.
The extinct wild cattle from which all domestic cattle descend.

gewusst: A bull does not see red as a bright colour, and in a bullfight he reacts to the waving of the cloth.
Through artificial insemination, a single breeding bull can become the father of tens of thousands of calves.

teile.einleitung: A surfactant is a substance that lowers the surface tension of water. Soap, washing-up liquid and washing powder contain surfactants so that they can dissolve grease and dirt. For animals such as the pond skater, however, a surfactant in the water can become a problem.
wichtigste: Surfactants lower the surface tension of water.
Soap is the oldest known surfactant.
A surfactant particle has a water-loving head and a grease-loving tail.
That is how surfactants can dissolve grease and dirt in water.
Pond skaters cannot walk on soapy water, because the soap weakens the surface tension.
Our lungs also make a natural surfactant.
Surfactants in waste water have to be biodegradable.

abschnitte.text: The German word, Tensid, comes from the Latin “tensio”, which means tension. A surfactant is a substance that gathers at the boundary between water and air or between water and grease. There it weakens the **surface tension**. Typical surfactants are found in soap, shampoo, washing-up liquid and laundry detergent.

Every surfactant particle has two ends. The **water-loving head** points towards the water, while the grease-loving tail hides in the grease or sticks out into the air. When washing, many particles surround a tiny droplet of grease and form small balls called **micelles**. That way the grease can be rinsed away with the water.

Pond skaters are insects that dart about on ponds and calm streams. Their legs carry fine, water-repellent hairs and spread their weight over the surface of the water. The surface tension acts like a thin, elastic skin. If you add soap to the water, this skin gets weaker, and the pond skater sinks in.

As long as 4000 years ago, the Sumerians in Mesopotamia made soap-like substances from fat and plant ash. Soap is made when fat is boiled with a lye, which is called **saponification**. In the 20th century, man-made surfactants were added, which also wash well in hard, chalky water. Today they are in almost every cleaning product.

Living things also make surfactants. In the air sacs of our lungs, a substance called **surfactant** makes sure that the tiny sacs do not stick together when we breathe out. Babies born very early often still have too little of it and therefore get help with breathing. The bile in our gut acts in a similar way and helps to digest fat from our food.

If many surfactants get into streams and lakes, they can harm fish, insects and other water animals. In Switzerland and in the EU, surfactants in detergents therefore have to break down easily. Waste water flows to the sewage works, where bacteria break the substances down. That is why you should not wash cars on the street and never pour washing-up water into a rain drain or into a stream.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force that holds the surface of water together like a thin skin.
A tiny ball made of many surfactant particles that encloses grease.
Making soap from fat and lye.
Can be broken down into harmless substances by bacteria and other living things.

gewusst: If you carefully lay a paper clip on water, it floats, but a drop of washing-up liquid makes it sink at once.
Soap bubbles exist only thanks to surfactants, and with pure water they burst at once.
Without the surfactant in the lungs, we would have to use much more effort with every breath.

teile.einleitung: The stone marten is a slender predator with greyish-brown fur that very much likes to live near people. It lives in attics, barns and sheds. It is known above all because it sometimes gnaws at cables in car engines.
wichtigste: The stone marten belongs to the marten family, like the badger and the weasel.
Its body is about 45 centimetres long without the tail.
It has greyish-brown fur and a white, forked patch on its throat.
In Switzerland it particularly likes to live in settlements, barns and attics.
It is active at night and eats almost anything, from mice to fruit.
The young are born blind and naked and are raised by the mother alone.
Many people regard it as a pest, but it also eats mice and rats.

abschnitte.text: The stone marten is about 45 centimetres long without the tail, and a bushy tail of about 25 centimetres is added to that. It usually weighs 1 to 2 kilograms. Its fur is **greyish brown**, and on its throat it has a white patch that forks downwards towards the front legs. In the closely related **pine marten** this throat patch is yellowish and rather rounded. Each paw has **five toes** with claws, with which it climbs superbly.

Stone martens live all over Europe and in parts of Asia. Originally they lived in rocky areas, hence the name. Today they are true **followers of human settlement** and live in villages and towns. In Switzerland they can be found in barns, woodpiles, garages and attics, from the Central Plateau up to the mountain villages.

The stone marten is an **omnivore**. It hunts mice, rats and birds and likes to eat eggs. In summer and autumn, cherries, plums, berries and insects are also on the menu. If it gets into a hen house, it can kill many hens, because the fluttering animals keep setting off its hunting instinct.

Mating takes place in summer, and at night you can hear cackling and screaming sounds. After that the embryo rests for several months, which is called **delayed implantation**.
