Only in spring, usually in March or April, are two to four young born. They are blind and naked, and only the female looks after them. After about five weeks they open their eyes.

In winter, stone martens sometimes look for a warm engine compartment, because the engine still gives off warmth after a drive. If a marten smells the scent of another marten there, it becomes furious and bites into cables and hoses. In this way it defends its **territory**. Such marten damage can be expensive. An engine wash that removes the scent and special deterrent devices can help.

Many people experience the stone marten as an annoying **pest**, because it thumps about in the attic at night and tears up insulation material. At the same time it is useful, because it eats many mice and rats. In Switzerland the stone marten is common and not endangered. It may be hunted during the hunting season.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wild animal that likes to live near people because it finds food and hiding places there.
A pause in the development of the embryo that moves the birth to spring.
The area that an animal claims for itself and defends against others of its kind.
The light patch on the neck and chest by which species of marten can be told apart.

gewusst: Although mating already takes place in summer, the young are only born around eight to nine months later.
A stone marten can slip through openings that are hardly bigger than a hen’s egg.

teile.einleitung: The tracheal system is the breathing system of insects. It consists of a network of fine little air tubes that run through the whole body and carry oxygen straight to the organs. Cockchafers, dung beetles and bees all breathe through tracheae.
wichtigste: Insects breathe with a tracheal system instead of lungs.
Cockchafers and dung beetles breathe through tracheae, fine little air tubes in the body.
The blood of insects carries hardly any oxygen.
Many insects actively pump air through their tracheae.
Flying insects often have extra air sacs.
The tracheal system limits how big insects can grow.
Marcello Malpighi described the tracheal system in the 17th century.

abschnitte.text: The tracheal system is a network of fine **little air tubes** that runs through the whole insect body. It begins at the breathing openings on the sides of the body and branches out as far as the individual cells. In this way oxygen gets directly to where it is needed. At the same time, carbon dioxide is carried out along the same route.

In small insects it is enough if the air spreads through the little tubes by itself, which is called **diffusion**. Larger insects move their abdomen like a bellows and so pump air in and out. Before taking off, the cockchafer visibly pumps with its abdomen several times to take on enough oxygen. Bees and other good fliers also have **air sacs**, which store air like small balloons.

In people, the blood carries oxygen from the lungs into the body. The blood of insects, the **haemolymph**, on the other hand, carries hardly any oxygen, because the tracheae do that job. That is why insect blood is mostly colourless, greenish or yellowish and not red. The heart of insects is a simple tube on the back.

abschnitte.titel: Limits and giants of prehistoric times
abschnitte.text: Because air moves forward only slowly through long tubes, insects cannot grow as big as they like. In the **Carboniferous**, about 300 million years ago, the air contained more oxygen than today. At that time there lived giant relatives of dragonflies such as Meganeura, with a wingspan of around 70 centimetres. Today the largest beetles, such as the goliath beetle, are only about as big as a hand.

The Italian researcher Marcello Malpighi examined the silkworm under the microscope in the 17th century and in doing so described the tracheae. Tracheal systems are found not only in insects but also in myriapods and some arachnids. Many spiders have **book lungs** as well as tracheae. Researchers think that tracheal systems arose several times independently in the course of evolution.

begriffe.erklaerung: The way a substance, for example air, spreads out by itself from places where there is a lot of it to places where there is little.
The blood of insects.
A widening of the tracheae that stores air.
A breathing organ of spiders with many thin leaves like the pages of a book.

gewusst: The pumping of the cockchafer before take-off is called “counting” in everyday German.
Some water insects carry an air bubble with them like a diving cylinder.
The larvae of dragonflies and mayflies breathe under water with tracheal gills.

teile.einleitung: The mallard is the most common and best-known duck in Switzerland. You can meet it on almost every lake, river and pond, even in the middle of town. The male with his shiny green head is easy to recognise.
wichtigste: The mallard is a dabbling duck and the ancestor of most domestic ducks.
The male is called a drake and has a shiny green head.
The female is speckled brown and well camouflaged.
Its feet are orange and have webbing between the toes.
With small combs on its bill it filters food out of the water.
It builds its nest on the ground, hidden in the grass near water.
Depending on the area, it is a migratory bird or a resident bird.

abschnitte.text: The mallard is about 50 to 60 centimetres long and weighs around a kilogram. The **drake** has a shiny green head, a white neck ring, a brown chest and a yellow bill. The female is speckled brown and is therefore well camouflaged when sitting on her eggs. Both have a blue, shimmering patch on the wing, the **speculum**. The feet are orange and have four toes, three of them joined by webbing.

Mallards live in Europe, Asia and North America almost everywhere there is water. They like lakes, rivers, streams, ponds and park ponds. In Switzerland many mallards breed here and stay all year round, and so they are **resident birds**. In winter, ducks from northern and eastern Europe, whose lakes freeze over, come here as well. Then many ducks also move to waters that stay free of ice.

The mallard is a **dabbling duck**. It does not dive right under, but puts its head and neck into the water and sticks its rear end up into the air. It eats water plants, seeds, snails, insect larvae and small crustaceans. With fine horny plates at the edge of its bill it sieves food out of the water. Bread is unhealthy for ducks and should not be fed to them.

The female builds a nest on the ground, hidden in the grass or under bushes near water. She usually lays 8 to 12 eggs and sits on them for about four weeks on her own. The ducklings are **nidifugous**, which means that they can walk and swim soon after hatching. They stay close to their mother, who calls them with a quiet quacking and protects them from enemies such as the fox. The mother also keeps them warm, especially on cool nights.

To preen, the duck takes oil from the **preen gland** at its tail with its bill and spreads it through its plumage. In this way the feathers stay waterproof. In summer the duck changes all its flight feathers at once and cannot fly for a few weeks. During this time even the drake looks plain brown, which is called eclipse plumage.

Almost all breeds of domestic duck descend from the mallard. The mallard is not endangered and is one of the most common ducks in the world. In Switzerland it may be hunted in the hunting season. Because it is not very shy, it is easy to watch, for example on Lake Zurich or on the River Aare.

begriffe.erklaerung: The male of a duck.
Searching for food in which a duck puts only its head and neck under water.
Young birds that can walk and leave the nest straight after hatching.
A gland above the tail whose oil makes the feathers waterproof.

gewusst: The quacking sound that we know from ducks is made mainly by the female, and the drake calls much more quietly.
During the moult in summer, a mallard cannot fly for several weeks.

teile.einleitung: A curry comb is a brush with short, firm studs or teeth that is used to clean the coat of horses. It loosens dirt, dust and loose hairs, which are then brushed away. Grooming with the curry comb is part of the daily care of a horse.
wichtigste: With the curry comb you brush the coat of a horse and remove dirt.
There are curry combs made of rubber, plastic and metal.
The rubber curry comb is moved over the coat in circular movements.
After that the dirt is brushed away with the dandy brush.
On the head and legs only soft brushes are used.
Grooming with a curry comb massages the skin and improves the blood flow.
While cleaning, you notice whether the horse has any injuries.

abschnitte.text: A curry comb is a cleaning tool, mainly for **horses**, but also for cattle. It is usually oval in shape with a strap for the hand. On the underside there are short rubber studs or rows of teeth. The German word striegeln means roughly to brush and clean vigorously.

The **rubber curry comb** is the most common and is used directly on the horse. Curry combs made of plastic are somewhat harder and suit a very dirty coat. The **metal curry comb** is mostly used only to comb out and clean the brushes. For the moulting season there are special curry combs that loosen a lot of hair at once.

You start at the neck and groom in small circles over the shoulder, back, belly and croup. In this way dirt and loose hairs come away. Then you brush in the direction of the hair with the **dandy brush**, a soft brush. From time to time you knock the curry comb clean. The head and lower legs are cleaned only with soft brushes, because the bones lie close under the skin there.

There must be no dirt under the saddle, or pressure sores can form. Grooming works like a **massage** and stimulates the blood flow. Many horses enjoy it and even stretch out their upper lip. While cleaning, you also discover small wounds, ticks or swellings early.

In spring and autumn horses change their coat. Then they lose especially many hairs, and grooming is especially important. Besides the curry comb you need a **hoof pick**, a dandy brush and a mane comb. Each horse should have its own grooming kit if possible, so that no skin diseases are passed on.

begriffe.erklaerung: A soft brush with dense bristles with which you brush the coat smooth after grooming with the curry comb.
A hook with which you remove stones and dirt from the hooves.
The change of coat in spring and autumn, in which animals lose a lot of hair.
The rear, upper part of a horse’s back above the hind legs.

gewusst: In many cowsheds today there are big, rotating brushes on which the cows can groom themselves.
In a herd, horses groom one another by nibbling at each other’s manes with their teeth.

teile.einleitung: The edible frog is a green water frog that lives in ponds, pools and puddles and puts on loud croaking concerts in early summer. It is one of the most widespread frog species in large parts of central Europe. What is especially exciting is that it is really a cross between two other frog species.
wichtigste: The scientific name of the edible frog is Pelophylax esculentus.
Today it belongs to the genus Pelophylax, the water frogs.
Its skin is mostly green with dark spots.
The males call with paired vocal sacs at the corners of the mouth.
It is mainly active during the day and likes to bask on the bank.
The strong hind legs, each with five toes, are important for jumping and fast swimming.
The female lays her eggs in lumpy clumps of spawn in the water.

abschnitte.text: The edible frog grows to about 7 to 10 centimetres long, and females are usually a little bigger than males. Its skin is **green with dark spots**, often with a light stripe down the middle of the back. The strong **hind legs** have five toes with webbing and are built for jumping and swimming. The eyes sit high on the head, so it can keep them above the water while its body is submerged.

The edible frog is a natural **hybrid**, that is, a cross between the marsh frog and the pool frog. It can only reproduce if it pairs with one of these parent species, mostly with the pool frog. In doing so it passes on the genes of only one parent species, a rare oddity in the animal kingdom. Since a new classification, all these water frogs belong to the genus **Pelophylax**.

Edible frogs live at sunny ponds, pools, gravel pits and slow-flowing ditches with plenty of water plants. They are mainly active **during the day** and like to bask on the bank or on water lily leaves. When in danger they leap into the water with a splash. They eat insects, spiders, worms and snails, and large ones even snap up smaller frogs.

On warm days in **spring and early summer**, especially in May and June, the loud calls can be heard from far away. The males inflate two whitish grey **vocal sacs** at the corners of the mouth, which strengthen the sound. The females lay their eggs in several lumpy **clumps of spawn** among water plants. Tadpoles hatch from them and turn into small frogs by late summer.

In autumn most edible frogs withdraw, some on land under leaves or into holes in the ground, others into the mud at the bottom of the water. There they spend the winter in **cold torpor**. Their heartbeat and breathing slow down greatly. In March or April they become active again.

Edible frogs need **clean water** for spawn and tadpoles, which is why polluted or drained ponds harm them especially. Released fish such as goldfish also eat eggs and tadpoles. In Switzerland all native amphibians are protected by law. In some areas the introduced marsh frog displaces the native water frogs, so natural ponds without fish are especially valuable.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals that live in water and on land, such as frogs, toads, newts and salamanders.
A cross between two different species.
Stretchy skin that blows up like a balloon when calling and strengthens the sound.
The eggs of frogs, toads or fish in the water.
The larva of a frog, which lives in water and breathes with gills.

gewusst: The name esculentus is Latin and means “edible”, because frogs' legs used to be eaten often from water frogs.
A chorus of edible frogs can be heard several hundred metres away at night.
Because it is a hybrid, the edible frog almost always lives together with one of its parent species at the same body of water.

teile.einleitung: The height at the withers, called “Stockmass” in German, is the height of a horse measured from the ground to the highest point of the withers. It is measured with a special measuring stick, hence the German name. In this way you know exactly how tall a horse is, and whether it counts as a pony, for example.
wichtigste: The height at the withers is used to measure the size of a horse in centimetres.
It is measured vertically from the ground to the withers.
The withers are the raised part where the neck meets the back.
A measuring stick with a horizontal arm is used for this.
According to competition rules, a pony is at most 148 centimetres tall.
In English-speaking countries, horses are often measured in the unit called the hand.
If measured with a tape measure, a slightly larger value is the result, the tape measurement.

abschnitte.titel: What is the height at the withers?
abschnitte.text: The “Stockmass” gives the **height at the withers** of a horse. The **withers** are the highest point on the back, where the neck turns into the back. The measurement is taken there because this spot hardly moves, unlike the head. The result is given in centimetres.

The horse stands on level, hard ground and puts its weight evenly on all four legs. The **measuring stick** is placed upright next to the horse. A horizontal arm is lowered until it rests on the withers. Then the height is read off on the scale.

According to the rules of the international equestrian federation, a horse up to 148 centimetres at the withers counts as a **pony**. Bigger animals are called horses. A Shetland pony is at most about 107 centimetres tall. Large heavy horses such as the Shire horse, on the other hand, can reach over 180 centimetres.

The best-known Swiss breed of horse is the **Franches-Montagnes** from the Jura. It usually has a height at the withers of about 150 to 160 centimetres. At breeding shows every horse is measured, and the height is entered in the horse passport. When buying a horse, too, the height at the withers is an important piece of information.

If you measure with a tape measure over the curve of the body, you get the **tape measurement**. It is a few centimetres larger than the height at the withers. In Great Britain, Ireland and America, horses are often measured in hands. One hand is equal to 4 inches, which is about 10.2 centimetres. For dogs, too, the size is given as height at the withers.

begriffe.erklaerung: The raised spot where a horse’s neck and back meet.
A rod with a scale and a sliding cross arm for measuring the height of a horse.
A small horse with a height at the withers of up to 148 centimetres.
A measurement taken with a flexible tape measure, which comes out slightly larger than the height at the withers.

gewusst: A horse of 16 hands is about 163 centimetres tall.
A horse is not measured at the head, because it keeps raising and lowering its head.

teile.einleitung: The green turtle is a large sea turtle that lives in warm seas all over the world. In German it is called Suppenschildkröte, or “soup turtle”, and it is also known as the green sea turtle, not because of its shell but because of its greenish body fat. As an adult it is almost purely a vegetarian and grazes on seagrass meadows like a cow on a field.
wichtigste: The green turtle (Chelonia mydas) is one of the sea turtles.
Its name “green sea turtle” comes from its greenish body fat.
Adult animals like to eat seagrass and algae best.
The shell can grow to over a metre long, and the animal often weighs well over 100 kilograms.
The females lay their eggs on sandy beaches, often on the beach where they hatched themselves.
The species is regarded as seriously endangered worldwide.

abschnitte.text: The green turtle has a flat, heart-shaped **carapace**, which is usually olive brown to grey. Adult animals are often 80 to 120 centimetres long. Instead of legs it has strong **flippers**, with which it glides elegantly through the water. Unlike land tortoises, it cannot pull its head and flippers back into its shell.

The green turtle lives in tropical and subtropical seas, for example in the Atlantic, the Pacific, the Indian Ocean and also in the eastern Mediterranean. It likes to stay in shallow coastal waters with **seagrass meadows** and coral reefs. Between feeding grounds and egg-laying beaches it often swims thousands of kilometres. The animals that travel from the coast of Brazil to the little island of Ascension in the middle of the Atlantic are famous.

Young green turtles also eat small animals such as jellyfish, snails and crustaceans. Adults become almost pure **plant eaters** and feed mainly on seagrass and algae. With their sharp-edged jaws they cut off the plants as if with scissors. Because they graze on the seagrass regularly, the seagrass meadows stay healthy and grow back well.

To lay their eggs, the females crawl at night on to a sandy beach and dig a deep hole with their hind flippers. In it they lay around 100 eggs each time, and they do so several times in a nesting season. After about two months the young hatch and crawl straight to the sea. The **temperature in the sand** decides whether an egg becomes a male or a female: warmer nests produce more females.

In the past the animals were caught in huge numbers, mainly for **turtle soup**, hence the German name Suppenschildkröte. Today they are threatened by fishing nets, plastic waste, built-up beaches and global warming. The species is protected internationally, and trade is banned by the **Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species** (CITES). The secretariat of this agreement has its seat in Geneva.

begriffe.erklaerung: A turtle that spends almost its whole life in the sea and comes on to land only to lay eggs.
A true flowering plant that grows under water on the seabed and forms large meadows.
An animal that feeds mainly on plants.
An international agreement that regulates trade in threatened animals and plants.

gewusst: While resting and sleeping under water, green turtles can hold their breath for several hours.
Whether an egg hatches as a male or a female depends not on genes but on the warmth of the sand.
Newly hatched young find their way by the bright horizon over the sea, which is why beach lamps confuse them.

teile.einleitung: Termites are small insects that live in huge colonies with a queen, a king, workers and soldiers. They look a little like ants, but are really close relatives of cockroaches. Some species build mounds that are taller than a person.
wichtigste: Today termites are counted in the insect order of cockroaches (Blattodea).
Their closest living relatives are the wood roaches of the genus Cryptocercus.
Around 3000 species of termite have been described worldwide.
The family with the most species is the Termitidae, the higher termites.
A termite colony has three main castes: reproductives, workers and soldiers.
Termites go through an incomplete metamorphosis without a pupa.
With the help of micro-organisms in the gut, many termites can digest wood.
The oldest reliably known termite fossils come from the Early Cretaceous.

abschnitte.text: The word “termite” comes from the Latin “termes”, which means woodworm. In the past, termites formed an order of their own called **Isoptera**, meaning “equal wings”, because the front and hind wings are the same size. Today we know that they belong to the cockroaches. Their closest relatives are the wood roaches of the genus **Cryptocercus**, which also eat wood and live in families.

Termites and ants both live in colonies, but they are not closely related. Termites go through an **incomplete metamorphosis**, so the young already look similar to the adults and there is no pupa. In ants all the workers are female, but in termites there are male and female workers. Also, in termites a king lives permanently in the nest alongside the queen.

A termite colony has three main castes: **reproductives**, workers and soldiers. The queen and king take care of the next generation, and in some species the huge queen lays several thousand eggs a day. The workers, which are mostly blind, collect food, look after the young and build the nest. The soldiers defend the colony with large jaws, or in some species squirt out sticky defensive substances.

Many tropical termites build mounds out of earth, saliva and droppings that can grow several metres high. A clever system of passages and shafts provides fresh air and an even temperature. Some African species lay out **fungus gardens** in the nest and feed on the fungus. In Australia the so-called compass termites build flat mounds that are lined up exactly north to south.

Termites eat mainly wood, leaves and other plant remains containing the tough substance cellulose. In doing so they are helped by tiny **micro-organisms** in their gut. In this way they break down dead plant material and make the soil fertile, much as earthworms do here. In wooden houses, however, they can cause great damage.

The oldest reliably known termite fossils come from the Early Cretaceous and are over 100 million years old. The Australian species **Mastotermes darwiniensis** is the only living species of its family. It lays its eggs in packets, similar to an ootheca in cockroaches, which shows how they are related. No native termites live in Switzerland, but there are a few species in southern Europe.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of animals in an insect colony with a particular job.
A firm substance that the walls of plant cells and wood are made of.
A protective egg case in which cockroaches lay their eggs.
Development from the egg through larvae to the adult animal without a pupal stage.
The older part of the Cretaceous period, about 145 to 100 million years ago.

gewusst: In some species a termite queen can live to be over ten years old, and she is much bigger than her workers.
In digesting, termites release the gas methane, a considerable amount worldwide.
Winged termites swarm out in their thousands after rain and shed their wings after landing.

teile.einleitung: The stone centipede is a nimble, brown centipede that lives in central Europe under stones, boards and rotting wood. If you turn over a stone in the garden, you often see it dash away in a flash. It is a small hunter that catches insects and spiders with its venom claws.
wichtigste: The stone centipede is one of the centipedes and is called Lithobius in science.
The best-known species is the brown centipede, which is very common in central Europe.
Adult stone centipedes usually have 15 pairs of legs.
It lives hidden under stones, wood, leaves and bark.
It hunts small animals such as insects, spiders and worms at night.
With its venom claws it paralyses its prey.
The stone centipede is harmless to humans.

abschnitte.text: The brown centipede grows to about 2 to 3 centimetres long. Its body is flat, shiny and reddish brown. Each body segment carries a pair of legs, and adult animals usually have **15 pairs of legs**. On its head are two long **antennae** with which it feels and smells. The last pair of legs is especially long and points backwards.

Stone centipedes need moisture, because otherwise they dry out quickly. That is why they hide during the day under **stones**, pieces of wood, flowerpots and in the leaf litter. They can be found in forests, gardens, parks and sometimes also in cellars. In Switzerland they are widespread on the Central Plateau and in the mountain valleys.

The stone centipede is a **predator** and hunts mainly at night. It eats insects, insect larvae, spiders, woodlice and small worms. Behind its head it has two modified legs, the **venom claws**. With them it seizes its prey and injects a venom that paralyses it.

The female lays her eggs one at a time and disguises each one with a little soil. The young hatch with only 7 pairs of legs. With every **moult** a new body segment with legs is added, until they have 15 pairs of legs. Stone centipedes can live for several years.

Stone centipedes are useful, because they eat many small pests in the soil. They only rarely stray into houses, and there they hardly find any food. Their bite can at most give people a slight nip and is not dangerous. They are among the **soil animals** that make up healthy garden soil.

begriffe.erklaerung: Jointed animals with many pairs of legs, exactly one pair on each body ring.
Modified legs behind the head with which centipedes seize and poison prey.
Shedding the old skin so that the animal can grow.
A single body ring, and the body is made up of many of them.

gewusst: Despite the name, no centipede has exactly a hundred legs, and the stone centipede has only 30.
If a stone centipede is threatened, it can drop a leg, which keeps twitching for a while and distracts the enemy.

teile.einleitung: A symbiosis is a close living-together of two different species in which both have an advantage. A famous example is the clownfish and the sea anemone. Symbioses are found everywhere in nature, even in your own tummy.
wichtigste: Symbiosis means two species living together for mutual benefit.
The clownfish finds protection in the sea anemone, and the anemone is cleaned and defended by it.
The word comes from Greek and means “living together”.
Lichens are a symbiosis between a fungus and an alga.
Bees and flowers help each other: the bee gets nectar, and the flower is pollinated.
In the human gut live billions of bacteria that help with digestion.

abschnitte.text: In a **symbiosis**, two different species live closely together, and both benefit from it. The term was introduced by the German scientist Heinrich Anton de Bary in 1879. Experts also call this mutual benefit **mutualism**. Some partners can no longer survive at all without each other, while others can also manage alone.

The sea anemone has poisonous stinging threads that paralyse other fish. The **clownfish** is protected by a special layer of mucus and can hide among the tentacles. In return it drives away fish that want to nibble at the anemone and keeps it clean. Its leftover food and droppings also serve the anemone as food.

**Lichens** on stones and tree bark consist of a fungus and an alga: the alga makes sugar, and the fungus gives support and stores water. Many trees in the Swiss forest live together with fungi whose threads wrap around the roots, which is called **mycorrhiza**. In Africa, oxpeckers pick ticks out of the fur of buffalo and rhinoceroses. And cows could not digest grass without the bacteria in their rumen.

People, too, live in symbiosis: in our gut live trillions of **bacteria**. They help to break down food, make vitamins and protect against disease germs. Even the power stations of our cells, the **mitochondria**, were independent bacteria a very long time ago. They were taken in by other cells and today are a permanent part of them.

Not every living-together benefits both sides. In **parasitism**, only one has an advantage and harms the other, like a tick or a tapeworm. In commensalism, one benefits and the other does not care, for example when birds nest in a tree. How important symbioses are is shown by coral bleaching: if corals lose their algae when the water is too warm, they turn white and can die.

begriffe.erklaerung: Two species living together, from which both benefit.
The technical word for a relationship with mutual benefit.
A living thing that lives at the expense of another and harms it.
Plant roots and fungi living together.

gewusst: Corals get the greatest part of their food from tiny algae that live in their tissue.
A person carries about as many bacteria in the gut as he or she has body cells.
Leafcutter ants grow fungus gardens in their nest and feed the fungi with pieces of leaf.

teile.einleitung: Deadwood is dead wood that stays in the forest, for example fallen trees, broken branches or old tree stumps. What looks like rubbish is in truth an important habitat. Thousands of beetles, fungi, birds and other living things depend on dead wood.
wichtigste: Deadwood is dead wood that stays in the forest.
A distinction is made between standing and lying deadwood.
In Switzerland about 6000 species depend on deadwood.
Beetles, fungi, woodpeckers and bats use deadwood.
As it decays, new, fertile forest soil is made.
A tree trunk often needs several decades before it has completely decayed.
Foresters now deliberately leave more deadwood lying in the forest.

abschnitte.text: Deadwood is the name for all the **dead wood** in the forest. This includes standing dead trees, fallen trunks, branches, root stocks and tree stumps. Dead parts on trees that are still alive, such as a broken branch, count as well. Standing deadwood is also called a **snag**.

abschnitte.titel: A habitat for thousands of species
abschnitte.text: In Switzerland about 6000 species depend on deadwood, which is about a fifth of all forest species. They include many beetles such as the **stag beetle**, the Rosalia longicorn and the rhinoceros beetle, whose larvae live in the wood for years. Many fungi such as the tinder fungus also grow on dead wood. Mosses, lichens, wild bees and ants also find a home there.

Woodpeckers such as the **black woodpecker** like to hammer their nest holes into rotten wood. Later, new tenants move into these holes, such as tits, nuthatches, owls, bats or edible dormice. Lying trunks offer hiding places for hedgehogs, mice, lizards and salamanders. In this way a dead tree is often more alive than a living one.

Fungi, bacteria, beetles and worms break down the wood bit by bit. This makes **humus**, that is, nutrient-rich earth on which new trees grow. A thick tree trunk often needs several decades, depending on the kind of wood and the climate, before it has completely decayed. In the mountain forest, young spruces even sprout on rotting trunks, which is called rejuvenation on decaying wood.

In the past, dead trees were cleared out of the forest, because the wood was needed and people wanted a tidy forest. Today we know how important deadwood is for **biodiversity**. That is why foresters deliberately leave habitat trees and deadwood standing and set up forest reserves in which nature is left to itself. In the mountain forest, lying trunks can also protect against falling rocks and avalanches.

begriffe.erklaerung: A dead tree that is still standing upright.
Dark, fertile earth made of decomposed plants and animals.
The great variety of different animal and plant species in an area.
A woodland area in which there is no felling or only a little, so that nature can develop freely.

gewusst: More living things can live in a dead tree trunk than in a living tree.
The larva of the stag beetle lives for several years in rotten wood before the beetle hatches.
Many rare beetles are on the Red List, because in managed forests there is too little old deadwood.

teile.einleitung: Thailand is a kingdom in South East Asia and is known for temples, beaches and a rich wildlife. Its national animal is the elephant, which has played a special part there for centuries. Tigers, gibbons and many colourful birds also live in its forests.
wichtigste: Thailand lies in South East Asia and is a kingdom.
The national animal of Thailand is the elephant.
The capital is Bangkok.
Until 1939 the country was called Siam.
Most people in Thailand are Buddhists.
Thailand has numerous national parks with rainforests and coral reefs.
The Siamese cat and the Siamese fighting fish come from Thailand.

abschnitte.text: Thailand lies between Myanmar, Laos, Cambodia and Malaysia and borders the Gulf of Thailand and the Andaman Sea. At around 513 000 square kilometres it is about twelve times as big as Switzerland. In the north there are mountains and forests, in the middle the fertile plain of the **Chao Phraya** river, and in the south a long peninsula with islands. The climate is tropical with a rainy season and a dry season.

The **Asian elephant** is the national animal of Thailand and a symbol of strength and good luck. In the past, elephants were used in war and for work in the forest, especially for carrying tree trunks. White elephants were regarded as sacred and belonged to the king, and the old flag of Siam showed a white elephant. Every year on 13 March, Thailand celebrates Elephant Day.

In Thailand live tigers, leopards, sun bears, gibbons, hornbills and many snakes and lizards. The seas off the coast have coral reefs with sea turtles and whale sharks. The Siamese **fighting fish** was named the national aquatic animal in 2019. The Siamese cat, too, takes its name from the old name of the country, Siam.

Thailand has over a hundred national parks. The oldest is the **Khao Yai National Park**, which was founded in 1962 and is a UNESCO World Natural Heritage Site. Wild elephants, gibbons and hornbills live there. Poaching and the felling of forests threaten many animal species, however.

Thailand is the only country in South East Asia that was never colonised by a European power. Since 2016 King Maha Vajiralongkorn, also called Rama X, has been the head of state. Around 70 million people live in the country (as of about 2024), and most of them speak **Thai** and are Buddhists. People pay with the baht.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal that is regarded as a symbol of a country.
The former name of Thailand.
A large, protected area for nature and animals.
A wind that brings the rainy season in southern Asia.

gewusst: The name Thailand means “land of the free”.
The full ceremonial name of Bangkok is regarded as one of the longest place names in the world.
In Thailand about as many elephants live in human care as in the wild.

teile.einleitung: The righting reflex is a lightning-fast, automatic movement with which an animal turns its body the right way up again. It is best known in the cat: if it falls, it turns in mid-air and almost always lands on its paws. It does not have to think about it, because its body does it all by itself.
wichtigste: A reflex is a movement that happens without thinking.
Righting reflexes make sure that the head and body get back into the right position.
In a falling cat, the head and front of the body turn first, and then the rest of the body follows.
The balance organ in the inner ear and the eyes report which way is up and which is down.
Young cats learn the righting reflex in their first weeks of life.
People also have righting reflexes, for example when they stumble.
A fall from a great height can still be dangerous for cats.

abschnitte.text: A **reflex** is a quick reaction of the body that happens without a conscious decision. Righting reflexes are special reflexes that bring the body back into its normal position. They help animals and people to keep their balance. In cats the righting reflex is especially well developed and has been famous for a long time.

abschnitte.titel: How does the cat sense its position?
abschnitte.text: In the inner ear lies the **balance organ**. Fluid moves in it when the head turns or tilts. Fine sensory hairs tell the brain at once which way is down. In addition, the eyes help to recognise the position.

First the cat turns its head until it is looking downwards. Then it turns the front of its body and pulls in its front legs so that the turn goes faster. Only then does the back of the body follow, because the cat is very **flexible** in the middle. Finally it stretches out all four legs and arches its back to soften the impact. All of this happens in fractions of a second.

In 1894 the French scientist **Étienne-Jules Marey** photographed a falling cat with many quick pictures one after another. In this way people could see for the first time exactly how it turns. Physicists were puzzled for a long time about how this is possible without pushing off anything. The solution: the cat turns the two halves of its body against each other and skilfully changes its shape as it does so.

Kittens do not have the righting reflex from birth. It develops from about the third or fourth week of life. At about seven weeks, young cats can do the turn reliably. In human **babies** too, doctors test certain righting reflexes to check their development.

Even if cats usually land on their paws, they can be badly hurt in falls. Injuries to the jaw, teeth and legs are common. If a cat falls from a window or off a **balcony**, it should be taken to the vet. That is why many cat owners secure windows and balconies with a net.

begriffe.erklaerung: A quick movement of the body that happens automatically and without thinking.
A small sense organ in the inner ear that senses the position and turns of the head.
The innermost part of the ear, in which the hearing organ and the balance organ lie.

gewusst: A falling cat can turn without pushing off anything, because it turns the front and back of its body one after the other.
The first series of photographs of a falling cat were taken over 130 years ago.

teile.einleitung: The side-striped jackal is a medium-sized predator of the dog family that lives in Africa. It gets its name from the light stripe that runs along each side of its body. It is shy, active at night and eats almost anything it finds.
wichtigste: The side-striped jackal lives in Africa south of the Sahara.
A light stripe on the side of the body is typical.
The tip of its tail is usually white.
It belongs to the dog family.
It eats small mammals, insects, fruit and carrion.
Side-striped jackals usually live together as a pair.
The species is regarded as not endangered.

abschnitte.text: The side-striped jackal is about as big as a medium-sized dog and weighs around 7 to 14 kilograms. Its fur is greyish brown. On each **side of the body** runs a light stripe with a dark edge below it. The tip of the tail is usually white. Its muzzle is slightly shorter and broader than in other jackals.

The side-striped jackal lives in West, Central, East and southern Africa. It likes damper **savannahs**, scrubland and light woodland. Open, dry grassland it mostly leaves to the black-backed jackal. It also lives near villages and fields.
The side-striped jackal is an **omnivore**. It eats mice, rats, hares, birds and insects. Fruit also makes up a large part of its food. Besides that it eats carrion and rubbish near settlements.

Side-striped jackals are active mainly at dusk and at night. A male and a female often live together for a long time as a **pair** and defend a shared territory. The three to six young are born in a den, often in an old den of an aardvark. Both parents bring food to the young.

In the past the side-striped jackal was counted in the genus Canis, which also includes the wolf and the dog. Today it is placed in a genus of its own together with the **black-backed jackal**. The black-backed jackal has a dark saddle on its back and a black tail tip. The **golden jackal** lives in Asia and south-eastern Europe and by now is also seen now and then in Switzerland.

begriffe.erklaerung: A medium-sized, dog-like predator from Africa, Asia or south-eastern Europe.
An animal that eats both meat and plants.
An area that an animal or a pair claims for itself and defends.
An African mammal that digs large burrows and eats termites.

gewusst: You can tell the side-striped jackal from the black-backed jackal, which has a black tail tip, by the white end of its tail.
Pairs of side-striped jackals often stay together for many years.

teile.einleitung: The star-nosed mole is a mole from North America with an incredible nose. Around its nostrils sit 22 pink feelers that look like a star. With this organ of touch it finds its prey in the dark in a flash.
wichtigste: The star-nosed mole lives in the east of Canada and in the north-east of the USA.
On its nose it has 22 feelers arranged like a star.
This sets it clearly apart from the European mole.
It lives in damp soil, marshes and on stream banks.
It can swim well and dives for food.
It eats worms, insect larvae and small water animals.
It is one of the fastest eaters in the whole animal kingdom.

abschnitte.text: The star-nosed mole is about 10 to 13 centimetres long, and a tail of 6 to 8 centimetres is added to that. It weighs only about 50 grams. Its dense fur is blackish brown and repels water. The most striking feature is the **nose star** made of 22 fleshy feelers. Its eyes are tiny, and it can hardly see anything.

The nose star is not an organ of smell but an **organ of touch**. On the feelers sit over 25 000 tiny touch buttons called **Eimer’s organs**. With them it senses the smallest prey animals in the ground. The star is more sensitive than the fingertips of a human.

The star-nosed mole lives in eastern North America, from Canada to the north-east of the USA. It likes damp meadows, **marshes**, bogs and the banks of streams and ponds. There it digs tunnels that often lead straight into the water. It does not live in Europe or in Switzerland.

It eats earthworms, insect larvae, small crustaceans, snails and sometimes small fish. With its star it touches the ground up to ten times a second. When it has felt something edible, it eats it in less than a quarter of a second. That makes it one of the fastest eaters among **mammals**.

The star-nosed mole can even smell under water. It blows small air bubbles out of its nose on to stones or prey and breathes them in again straight away. In this way it picks up **scent substances** from the water. This ability was unknown in mammals for a long time.

The star-nosed mole does not hibernate and even dives under the ice for food. In winter its tail grows thicker, because it stores fat in it as a **store**. In spring, usually four to five young are born. The species is regarded as not endangered.

begriffe.erklaerung: A part of the body with which an animal can feel touch especially finely.
Tiny touch buttons in the skin of moles, named after the scientist Theodor Eimer.
Small mammals that mostly live underground and dig tunnels.

gewusst: The nose star has more touch-sensing cells than the whole human hand.
The star-nosed mole can smell under water by blowing out air bubbles and breathing them in again.

teile.einleitung: The ostriches are a family of large, flightless birds from Africa. They include the largest bird in the world, the ostrich. They count among the running birds, which, instead of flying, run on long, strong legs.
wichtigste: The ostrich is the largest bird in the world, but cannot fly.
The ostrich family today includes two species, the common ostrich and the Somali ostrich.
Ostriches belong to the group of running birds.
Related running birds are the emu, rhea, cassowary and kiwi.
Running birds have a flat breastbone without a keel for strong flight muscles.
In the past, ostriches also lived in Asia and on the Arabian Peninsula.
Ostriches lay the largest eggs of all living birds.

abschnitte.text: The ostriches form a bird family of their own with the scientific name Struthionidae. Today only two species still live, the **common ostrich** and the **Somali ostrich**. Both live in Africa. A fully grown ostrich can grow to about 2.5 metres tall and is thus the largest living bird.

Ostriches are far too heavy to fly. Their **breastbone** is flat and has no keel to which strong flight muscles could attach. Their feathers are soft and loose, and they do not hold together as in flying birds. In return they have very strong legs and are among the fastest runners on two legs.

Ostriches belong to the **running birds**, which are spread over the southern continents. The emu lives in Australia, the cassowary in New Guinea and northern Australia, and the rhea in South America. The small kiwi from New Zealand is also a running bird. The giant **moas** from New Zealand and the elephant bird from Madagascar are extinct.

Fossils show that ostriches used to be much more widespread. During the ice ages they also lived in Asia, for example in China and India. On the Arabian Peninsula there was the Arabian ostrich until the 20th century. It was wiped out by hunting.

At about 1.5 kilograms, ostriches lay the heaviest eggs of all living birds. Several females often lay their eggs in a shared **nest**, a shallow hollow in the sand. The male and the main hen take turns sitting on the eggs. The chicks can walk soon after hatching and grow very quickly.

Even in ancient Egypt, ostrich feathers were prized. In the 19th and early 20th centuries they were so popular as decoration for ladies’ hats that people began to keep ostriches on **farms**. Today they are bred for meat, leather and feathers, also in Europe and Switzerland. Blown-out ostrich shells were used as water containers thousands of years ago.

begriffe.erklaerung: Flightless birds with strong legs, also called ratites.
A bony ridge on the breastbone to which the flight muscles of flying birds attach.
Petrified remains of animals or plants from earlier times.
In biology, a group of related genera and species.

gewusst: The ostrich lays the largest egg of all birds, but in proportion to its body it is one of the smallest.
The extinct elephant bird from Madagascar laid eggs that were much bigger still than ostrich eggs.

teile.einleitung: The tamarind is a large tropical tree whose brown pods contain a sweet and sour fruit pulp. Its fruits are among the favourite foods of the ring-tailed lemurs of Madagascar. People in many countries also use it to flavour and sweeten their dishes.
wichtigste: The tamarind (Tamarindus indica) is a tree from the legume family.
It originally comes from tropical Africa and is grown today in many warm countries.
Its fruits are brown pods with sticky, sweet and sour pulp.
The fruit of the tamarind tree is among the favourite foods of ring-tailed lemurs.
The name comes from Arabic and means “Indian date”.
Tamarind is an important ingredient in Indian, Thai and Mexican cooking.

abschnitte.text: The tamarind is an evergreen tree that can grow over 20 metres tall. It has a broad, shady crown and **feathery leaves** made of many small leaflets. The flowers are yellowish with red stripes. Tamarind trees grow slowly, but can live to a great age and cope well with dry seasons.

The fruits are brown, slightly curved **pods**, about 5 to 15 centimetres long. Under the brittle shell lies a sticky, brown **fruit pulp** with hard seeds. It tastes sweet and sour at the same time, because it contains a lot of sugar and fruit acid. The tamarind belongs to the legumes and is therefore related to beans and peas.

abschnitte.titel: Favourite food of the ring-tailed lemurs
abschnitte.text: In Madagascar, tamarind trees grow mainly in the dry forests in the south of the island. There live the **ring-tailed lemurs**, lemurs with a black and white ringed tail. They eat fruit, leaves and flowers of the tamarind, and in some seasons it makes up a large part of their food. In zoos too, for example in Switzerland, ring-tailed lemurs like to be given fruit as a treat.

In India tamarind goes into curries, chutneys and soups. In Thailand it is an ingredient of the noodle dish **Pad Thai**, and in Mexico people drink chilled tamarind water. The well-known **Worcestershire sauce** from England also contains tamarind. In Swiss Asian shops you can buy it as a paste or as whole pods.

The tamarind originally comes from tropical **Africa**. A long time ago it reached India, where it is so widespread that people thought it was native. Arab traders therefore called it “tamr hindi”, that is, **Indian date**. Later the Spanish and Portuguese brought it to Central and South America.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plant family whose fruits grow in pods, like beans, peas and the tamarind.
A lemur from Madagascar with a black and white ringed tail.
Soft, mushy flesh of a fruit.
A plant that has leaves all year round.

gewusst: Tamarind pulp was also used in the past to polish brass and copper, because its acid dissolves stains.
In the morning, ring-tailed lemurs sunbathe with their arms spread out, as if they were meditating.
Despite its name “Indian date”, the tamarind is not related to the date palm.

teile.einleitung: The Tatra chamois is a rare subspecies of the chamois that lives only in the High Tatras, a high mountain range on the border between Slovakia and Poland. It is closely related to the chamois in the Swiss Alps. Because at times there were only a few hundred animals left, it is strictly protected.
wichtigste: The Tatra chamois (Rupicapra rupicapra tatrica) is a subspecies of the chamois.
It lives only in the Tatras in Slovakia and Poland.
Around the year 2000 there were only a few hundred animals left.
Thanks to strict protection, the population has grown again to over a thousand animals.
It is a symbol of the Tatra national parks.
Like all chamois, it climbs surely on steep rock.

abschnitte.text: The **Tatras** are the highest mountain range of the Carpathians, and their highest peak is Gerlachovský štít at about 2655 metres. Here the Tatra chamois lives on rock faces, scree slopes and alpine meadows above the tree line. In winter it often comes down a little lower, where it finds food more easily. Outside the Tatras this **subspecies** is not found naturally anywhere.

The Tatra chamois looks very much like the Alpine chamois. Both sexes have short, black, hook-shaped **horns** that curve backwards, which in German are called Krucken. In summer the coat is reddish brown, and in winter it is dense and almost black. Typical is the light face with a dark stripe from the horn over the eye to the mouth.

Chamois eat grasses, herbs, lichens, buds and in winter also needles and shoots. The females live with the young in **herds**, older bucks often alone. In late autumn is the mating season, which is called the **rut**. In early summer a single young one is usually born, which can climb after only a few hours.

Through hunting, poaching and disturbance by tourism, the population shrank sharply. Around the year 2000 only a few hundred animals lived in the Tatras. The **national parks** on the Slovak and Polish sides protect the animals together and count them every year. By now clearly over a thousand Tatra chamois live in the mountains again, and the animal appears in the logo of the Polish Tatra National Park.

In the Swiss Alps and in the Jura lives the **Alpine chamois**, the most common subspecies. There are about 90 000 chamois in Switzerland. Here they are popular game, and the long tuft of back hair of the bucks is worn on hats as a **Gamsbart**, a chamois beard. The Tatra chamois, on the other hand, is so rare that it may not be hunted at all.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group within an animal species that lives in a particular area and differs a little.
The hook-shaped horns of the chamois.
The mating season in deer, chamois and other hoofed animals.
A large protected area in which nature is allowed to develop as undisturbed as possible.

gewusst: Chamois can stand on almost vertical rock faces because their hooves have hard edges and a soft, grippy sole.
The High Tatras are much smaller than the Alps, but are regarded as the smallest high mountain range in the world with a truly alpine character.
The Slovak Tatra National Park was founded in 1949 and is the oldest national park in Slovakia.

teile.einleitung: Rabies is a dangerous viral disease that attacks the brain and can be passed on from animals to people. In Switzerland dogs are vaccinated against rabies regularly. Thanks to vaccinations, Switzerland is regarded today as free of rabies in land animals.
wichtigste: Rabies is a viral disease that attacks the nervous system.
It is mostly passed on through bites and the saliva of infected animals.
Dogs are vaccinated regularly against rabies in Switzerland.
Once the disease breaks out, it almost always ends in death.
A vaccination soon after a bite can prevent the disease from breaking out.
Louis Pasteur developed the first rabies vaccine for people in 1885.
Switzerland defeated fox rabies with vaccine baits.

abschnitte.text: Rabies is caused by a **virus** that belongs to the lyssaviruses. The virus travels along the nerves to the brain. Sick animals often become restless, aggressive or lose their fear of people, while others become dull and paralysed. The German word for rabies, Tollwut, uses “toll”, which used to mean “mad”.

Rabies is passed on mainly through **bites**, because the virus is in the saliva. Worldwide, dogs are the most important source of infection for people. In Europe it used to be mainly foxes that played a big part. Bats can also carry rabies viruses, which is why you should never touch sick or injured bats with bare hands.

There is an effective **vaccination** against rabies for animals and people. The first vaccine for people was used by Louis Pasteur in 1885 on nine-year-old Joseph Meister, who had been bitten by a rabid dog. If someone is bitten, they must go to a doctor at once, because a quick vaccination prevents the disease from breaking out. Dogs and cats that travel abroad need a valid rabies vaccination.

In 1967 fox rabies reached Switzerland from Germany. In 1978 researchers in the Valais laid out **vaccine baits** for foxes for the first time anywhere in the world, that is, chicken heads containing vaccine. This method was so successful that it was later taken up all over Europe. Since 1999 Switzerland has been regarded as free of rabies in land animals, although the virus still very rarely occurs in bats.

Worldwide an estimated 59 000 people or so die of rabies every year, mainly in Asia and Africa. Many of them are children who were bitten by dogs. The World Health Organization wants to make sure that nobody dies of rabies from dogs any more. **World Rabies Day** on 28 September reminds people of this disease every year.

begriffe.erklaerung: A tiny germ that causes disease and can multiply only inside living cells.
A lump of food containing vaccine that wild animals eat and are protected by.
The fluid in the mouth, also called spit.
A substance that teaches the body to fight off a disease.

gewusst: Switzerland was the first country in the world to vaccinate foxes against rabies with vaccine baits.
An old German word for rabies is “Hundswut”, meaning dog madness.
Because people with rabies often get spasms when swallowing, they used to be said to have a “fear of water”.

teile.einleitung: Myriapods, in German called Tausendfüsser or “thousand-footers”, are arthropods with a long body of many similar rings, on which many legs sit. They include the nimble centipedes and the slow-moving millipedes, which you find under leaves, stones and wood. By the way, not a single species has exactly a thousand legs.
wichtigste: Myriapods belong to the arthropods, like insects, spiders and crustaceans.
The group is called Myriapoda in science and includes centipedes, millipedes, pauropods and symphylans.
Their body consists of many similar trunk segments with legs.
No myriapod has exactly a thousand legs, and most have far fewer.
In central Europe they mostly live in the soil, under leaves, stones and wood.
They need moisture and are mostly active at night, because otherwise they dry out easily.
Myriapods have existed for about 420 million years, and they are among the first land animals.

abschnitte.text: Myriapods or **Myriapoda** are a group of **arthropods** with over 15 000 known species worldwide. Their body consists of a head and a long trunk made up of many identically built sections, the **segments**. Unlike insects, they therefore do not have a trunk made of a chest and an abdomen with only six legs. On the head they have a pair of antennae, with which they mainly feel and smell.

The **centipedes** have one pair of legs per segment and are fast predators with venom claws on the head. The **millipedes** have two pairs of legs on most segments and eat mainly rotting plants. Added to these are the tiny, soft **pauropods** and **symphylans**, which grow to only a few millimetres. The number of legs ranges, depending on the species, from about 20 to over 1000.

In central Europe, myriapods live in the soil, under leaves, stones, bark and dead wood. Their skin has no waterproof layer of wax as insects have, so they **dry out easily**. That is why most are out and about at night, when it is cooler and damper. Some species have simple eyes, but many are blind and find their way with their antennae.

Millipedes break up fallen leaves and dead wood and so help to form fertile **humus**. Centipedes hunt insects, spiders and worms and keep their numbers in check. To defend themselves, some millipedes such as the pill millipede roll up into a ball. Others give off foul-smelling or caustic fluids to scare off enemies.

In Swiss gardens and woods you often find the brown **stone centipede**, a nimble centipede. Under leaves live flat-backed and snake millipedes that coil up in a spiral when disturbed, and the rolling pill millipedes. In Ticino, and increasingly also north of the Alps, the long-legged **house centipede** is found in houses. The native species are harmless to people.

Myriapods have existed for about 420 million years, which makes them among the oldest known land animals. A fossil millipede from Scotland is one of the earliest animals that breathed air. In the Carboniferous, about 300 million years ago, lived the giant myriapod **Arthropleura**, which could grow over two metres long. It is the largest known arthropod that ever lived on land.

begriffe.erklaerung: Animals with a hard outer skeleton and jointed legs, such as insects, spiders, crustaceans and myriapods.
One of the many similar sections that make up the body.
The scientific name of the myriapods, meaning “countless feet”.
Dark, fertile soil made of decomposed plant remains.

gewusst: Only in 2021 was a myriapod discovered in Australia, Eumillipes persephone, that really has over a thousand legs, namely up to 1306.
Young millipedes hatch with only a few pairs of legs and get new segments and legs with every moult.
Some tropical centipedes grow over 25 centimetres long and even catch mice and bats.

teile.einleitung: The Animal Welfare Act is a federal law that sets out in Switzerland how people have to treat animals. It protects the dignity and well-being of animals. Among other things, it also regulates the duty to mark dogs with a microchip.
wichtigste: The Animal Welfare Act protects the dignity and well-being of animals.
The current law dates from 2005 and has been in force since 1 September 2008.
More detailed rules are set out in the Animal Welfare Ordinance.
Among other things, the law regulates the duty to mark dogs with a microchip.
Social animals such as guinea pigs may not be kept alone.
The cantonal veterinary offices are responsible for checks.
Since 2003 animals are no longer regarded as things in Swiss law.

abschnitte.text: The Animal Welfare Act, TSchG for short in German, is a law of the Confederation. It applies to all vertebrates and to some invertebrates such as octopuses and decapod crustaceans. The aim is to protect the **dignity** and well-being of animals. Nobody may cause an animal pain, suffering or fear without reason.

The first federal animal welfare law came into force in 1978. The current law was passed on 16 December 2005 and came into force on 1 September 2008. As early as 1992, Switzerland wrote the “dignity of creatures” into its Federal Constitution, as one of the first countries in the world. Exact rules, for example how big an enclosure has to be, are set out in the **Animal Welfare Ordinance**.

Anyone who keeps an animal has to feed it properly, care for it and give it enough space and things to do. Social animals such as guinea pigs, rabbits or budgerigars may not be kept alone. Dogs have to be marked with a **microchip** and registered in the Amicus database. Docking, that is, cutting off the ears or tail of dogs, is forbidden.

Cows, pigs and hens are protected as well, for example through minimum sizes for stables and rules for transport. Many Swiss rules go further than those of neighbouring countries. **Animal experiments** are allowed only with a permit and have to be well justified. A commission checks whether the benefit is greater than the suffering of the animals.

The **cantonal veterinary offices** are responsible for checks. Anyone who tortures or neglects animals can be punished, in serious cases even with prison. The authorities can take animals away from a keeper and forbid them to keep animals. Anyone who sees cruelty to animals can report it to the veterinary office.

begriffe.erklaerung: The idea that animals have a value of their own and must be treated with respect.
A supplement to a law with exact details.
A cantonal authority for animal welfare and animal health.
A chip the size of a grain of rice under the skin with a number that can be used to find the keeper.

gewusst: Anyone who kept a dog in Switzerland was required between 2008 and 2016 to attend a dog course.
Since 2003 the Swiss Civil Code has included the sentence that animals are not things.
Since 2018, lobsters may also no longer be thrown alive into boiling water in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The Toggenburg goat is a Swiss breed of goat from the Toggenburg in the canton of St Gallen. You can recognise it by its brown coat with white stripes on the face. It is a good dairy goat and is kept all over the world today.
wichtigste: The Toggenburg goat comes from the Toggenburg in the canton of St Gallen.
Its coat is mostly brown with white stripes on the face.
It is a dairy goat.
Most Toggenburg goats have no horns.
The breed has been exported to many countries, for example to England and the USA.
Switzerland has many breeds of goat of its own.

abschnitte.text: The coat of the Toggenburg goat is mostly light brown to mouse grey. Typical are two **white stripes** on the face, running from the eyes to the muzzle. The ears are also edged in white, and the lower legs and the area around the tail are white. Most animals are **hornless**, and some have small flaps of skin on the neck that are called wattles.

The breed comes from the **Toggenburg**, the valley of the upper Thur between the Säntis and the Churfirsten in the canton of St Gallen. There farming families have kept goats for milk and meat for a long time. In the 19th century the breed was bred on purpose and recorded in a herd book. The aim was a hardy goat that gives plenty of milk even in the harsh mountain climate.

The Toggenburg goat is an excellent **dairy goat**. A nanny gives several hundred litres of milk a year. Cheese, yoghurt and butter are made from goat's milk, and it tastes a little stronger than cow's milk. Because the goat is hardy and calm, it is also well suited to small farms and hobby keepers.

From the late 19th century, Toggenburg goats were taken to Great Britain, the USA and many other countries. There, lines of their own were developed, such as the British Toggenburg. In America the Toggenburg is among the best-known dairy goats. In Switzerland itself the breed is now rarer than the white **Saanen goat**.

Switzerland has a surprising number of breeds of goat of its own. They include the Saanen goat, the Chamois Coloured goat, the Appenzell goat, the Grisons Striped goat, the Valais Blackneck goat and the Peacock goat. Some of these breeds are rare and are supported by the foundation **Pro Specie Rara**. Goats are ruminants and good climbers.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of domestic animals with the same typical features.
The Swiss word for a female goat, and its young is called a Gitzi.
A breeding book in which the ancestry and performance of the animals are recorded.
An animal that brings its food back up and chews it a second time.

gewusst: Goats are among the oldest domestic animals and were tamed in the Near East as long ago as about 10 000 years.
The male goat is called a buck and smells very strong in the breeding season.
Goats can even climb sloping trees to reach leaves.

teile.einleitung: The Bactrian camel is a camel with two humps that lives in the cold deserts and steppes of Central Asia. It can stand scorching heat in summer and icy cold in winter. For thousands of years Bactrian camels have carried loads through the Gobi Desert.
wichtigste: The Bactrian camel has two humps.
It is a mammal and belongs to the camel family.
The humps store mainly fat, not water.
Wild Bactrian camels now live only in desert areas of Mongolia and China.
Broad feet with calloused soles stop it from sinking into the sand.
In a sandstorm it can close its nostrils.
A female usually gives birth to a single young one.

abschnitte.text: The Bactrian camel is a large **mammal** with two humps on its back. The shoulder height is about 1.80 to 2.30 metres, and fully grown animals weigh several hundred kilograms. The feet are broad and have **calloused soles**, so that the animal does not sink into the sand. Long eyelashes protect the eyes, and in a sandstorm it can close its nostrils.

Bactrian camels live in Central Asia, where the summers are hot and the winters bitterly cold. Their name in many languages recalls the old region of **Bactria**, which lay in the area of present-day Afghanistan. Wild Bactrian camels now live only in desert areas of Mongolia and China, mainly in the Gobi Desert. These wild camels are regarded today as a separate species and are critically endangered.

Bactrian camels eat grasses, shrubs and even thorny or salty plants that other animals avoid. The humps store mainly **fat**, not water. When the animal goes hungry for a long time, the humps become floppy and tip to the side. If it has the chance to drink, a thirsty camel can take in over a hundred litres of water in a few minutes.

In winter the Bactrian camel wears a thick, long coat that protects it from temperatures far below zero. In spring it loses the thick **winter coat** in large tufts. People collect this wool and make warm blankets and clothes from it. In summer the animal therefore often looks a little scruffy.

The mating season of Bactrian camels is in winter. After a gestation of about 13 months, the female usually gives birth to a single young one. The foal can walk just a few hours after birth. It drinks its mother's milk for over a year.

The domestic camel was tamed several thousand years ago and was an important pack animal on the **Silk Road**. As a pack animal it can carry from several dozen up to about 200 kilograms. People in Mongolia still use Bactrian camels today for milk, meat, wool and as animals to ride. By contrast, the dromedary from Arabia and North Africa has only one hump.

begriffe.erklaerung: A raised part on the back of the camel in which fat is stored.
A thick, soft pad of hard skin on the underside of the foot.
The one-humped camel from Arabia and North Africa.
A very old network of trade routes between China and Europe.

gewusst: The red blood cells of camels are oval and not round as in other mammals.
Bactrian camels can stand temperatures of about minus 40 to plus 40 degrees Celsius.
Memory aid: the Bactrian camel has two humps like the letter B for Bactria, and the dromedary has one like the letter D.

teile.einleitung: The housefly is the fly that buzzes through kitchens and living rooms in summer. It is found almost everywhere that people live, and in warm weather it multiplies at lightning speed. It does not bite, but it can pass on disease germs.
wichtigste: The housefly is called Musca domestica in science.
It is found almost everywhere in the world where people live.
Its buzzing comes from its fast wingbeat.
With its compound eyes it spots movement very quickly.
A white larva, the maggot, hatches from the egg.
In warm weather it develops so quickly that there are several generations in one summer.
The housefly does not bite and does not drink blood.

abschnitte.text: The housefly is about 6 to 7 millimetres long. Its chest is grey with four dark stripes along its length, and the abdomen is yellowish to grey. Like all flies it has only two wings, and the rear pair of wings has turned into tiny **halteres**. These help it to keep its balance in flight. Its big red **compound eyes** are made up of thousands of single eyes.

The housefly is found almost all over the world where people live. In German it is called Stubenfliege, or “living-room fly”, because it often turns up in homes, in the living room. There are especially many near stables, compost heaps and rubbish. There it finds food and places for its eggs.

The housefly has a **sponging proboscis** with which it can only soak up liquid food. Solid food such as sugar it dissolves by putting saliva on it. It likes sweet things, but also rubbish, droppings and spoiled food. With sensory hairs on its feet it can even taste.

The female lays several hundred eggs in damp dung, compost or rubbish. White, legless **maggots** hatch from them. They eat and grow and after a few days pupate in a brown barrel-shaped pupa. In summer warmth the whole development from egg to fly takes only about ten days. That is why there are several **generations** in one summer.

The housefly beats its wings very fast, about 200 times a second, and you hear this as buzzing. Its eyes take in many more pictures per second than ours. That is why it sees a hand swatting at it coming as if in slow motion. With sticky pads on its feet it can even walk on the ceiling and on window panes.

Because houseflies land on droppings and rubbish and afterwards on food, they can pass on **disease germs**. That is why you should cover food and keep rubbish closed. Fly screens on the windows keep them out. For many animals, such as spiders, swallows and other birds, flies are an important food.

begriffe.erklaerung: An eye made up of many small single eyes, typical of insects.
The legless larva of a fly.
Tiny, modified hind wings with which flies keep their balance in flight.
All the animals that are born at about the same time, for example parents or children.

gewusst: Houseflies taste with their feet as soon as they land on something.
To a housefly, a hand racing towards it looks as if it is in slow motion.

teile.einleitung: A wallow is a muddy hollow or puddle in which animals roll about. Wild boar, deer, bison, elephants and rhinoceroses like to bathe in mud. What looks dirty to us is personal care for them.
wichtigste: A wallow is a hollow with mud or water in which animals roll about.
Bison roll in wallows, and so do wild boar and deer.
A mud bath cools the body on hot days.
The layer of mud protects against insects, parasites and sunburn.
Rolling about in the mud is called wallowing.
After wallowing, wild boar rub themselves against trees, so-called rubbing trees.
Wallows are also habitats for frogs, newts and insects.

abschnitte.text: A wallow is a shallow hollow in the ground in which rainwater and mud collect. Animals lie down in it and roll about until their whole body is covered with mud. This behaviour is called **wallowing**. Many wallows are used again and again over the years and become deeper and deeper.

**Wild boar** and domestic pigs are well known for wallowing. Red deer also like to wallow, especially during the rutting season in autumn. In North America **bison** roll in hollows of mud or dust. In Africa and Asia, elephants, rhinoceroses, buffalo and hippopotamuses wallow.

Pigs can hardly sweat, so they cool down in the mud. The drying mud forms a protective layer against flies, horseflies, **ticks** and sunburn. When the mud later falls off, it takes parasites with it. When wallowing, deer also leave behind their scent and in this way show other deer that they are there.

After the mud bath, wild boar rub themselves against a tree nearby, the **rubbing tree**. As a result the bark of these trees is crusted with mud and rubbed smooth up to a certain height. Foresters and hunters can tell from this how big the wild boar in the area are. In Swiss woods you often find such trees next to wallows.

Wallows are small wetlands in the middle of the forest or the prairie. Tadpoles, newts, dragonfly larvae and water beetles live in them. In Switzerland, for example, the rare **yellow-bellied toad** and the alpine newt benefit from such puddles. The old bison wallows in the North American prairie still fill with rainwater today and provide a habitat for many plants and animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: An animal rolling about in the mud.
A tree against which wild boar rub themselves after a mud bath.
Living things such as ticks or lice that live on or in another animal and harm it.
The mating season in deer.

gewusst: Pigs have almost no sweat glands and therefore wallow to avoid overheating.
From the mud on a rubbing tree you can tell how big the wild boar in the area are.

teile.einleitung: The Syrian brown bear is a subspecies of the brown bear that lives in parts of Western Asia. It is also called the Syrian bear and is one of the smaller and lightest forms of brown bear. One of these bears even became famous as a “soldier” in the Second World War.
wichtigste: The Syrian brown bear (Ursus arctos syriacus) is a subspecies of the brown bear.
It lives in parts of Western Asia, for example in Turkey, Iran and the Caucasus.
Its fur is often light, straw-coloured to light brown.
It is one of the smaller brown bears.
It is an omnivore and eats mainly plants, fruit and nuts.
In Syria and Lebanon it is extinct or extremely rare today.

abschnitte.text: The Syrian brown bear is smaller than, for example, the grizzly or the Kodiak bear. Its dense fur is usually **light**, often straw yellow, sandy or light brown, and the legs are sometimes darker. Like all brown bears it has a powerful hump on its shoulders and long **claws** for digging. Males are clearly bigger and heavier than females.

The Syrian brown bear lives in mountain forests and mountain ranges of **Western Asia**. Today it is found mainly in Turkey, Iran, the Caucasus with Georgia, Armenia and Azerbaijan, and in the north of Iraq. In the past it also lived in Syria, in Lebanon and in the area of present-day Israel. There it was wiped out or almost wiped out by hunting and loss of habitat.

The bear is an **omnivore**, but eats mostly plant food. Its menu includes grasses, roots, berries, fruit and nuts. Added to these are insects, larvae, honey and occasionally small mammals or carrion. In autumn it eats its way to a thick layer of fat before it goes into its **winter rest**.

In 1942, Polish soldiers in Iran bought a bear cub, a Syrian brown bear. They called him **Wojtek** and took him along on their journey through the Middle East as far as Italy. He was officially listed as a soldier and is said to have helped to carry crates of ammunition. After the war Wojtek lived in Edinburgh Zoo in Scotland until his death in 1963.

abschnitte.titel: Threats and the link to Switzerland
abschnitte.text: The Syrian brown bear is threatened by poaching, logging and conflicts with farmers. In many countries it is protected, and some animals live in zoos and bear parks. In Switzerland there are no Syrian brown bears in the wild. Here the last native **brown bear** was shot in 1904 in the Lower Engadine, and today bears from the Italian Trentino wander in now and then.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group within an animal species that lives in a particular area and looks a little different.
An animal that eats both plants and animals.
A long sleep in winter in which the body saves energy but does not cool down as much as in hibernation.
An area in the west of Asia, for example Turkey, Iran, Iraq and Syria.

gewusst: The bear Wojtek was given a rank of his own in the Polish army and reportedly liked to drink beer.
Bears in old stories from the Middle East probably mean the Syrian brown bear.
Like all brown bears, the Syrian brown bear can run very fast over short distances despite its size.

teile.einleitung: Fresh water is water that contains hardly any salt, as in streams, rivers, lakes and groundwater. For many animals it is the most important habitat, for example for the whitefish in the Swiss lakes. Although the Earth is a blue planet, only a very small part of its water is fresh water.
wichtigste: Fresh water contains less than one gram of salt per litre.
Only about 2.5 to 3 per cent of all the water on Earth is fresh water, and most of that is frozen as ice.
The whitefish of the Swiss lakes live in fresh water.
A distinction is made between flowing waters such as streams and rivers and still waters such as lakes and ponds.
Freshwater animals constantly have to get rid of excess water from their bodies.
Switzerland is called the “water tower of Europe” because of its many springs, lakes and glaciers.

abschnitte.text: In seawater about 35 grams of salt per litre are dissolved on average. **Fresh water**, on the other hand, contains less than one gram of salt per litre, which is why it does not taste salty. Where rivers flow into the sea, the two mix to form **brackish water**. Fresh water comes mainly from rain and snow, because when water evaporates, the salt stays behind in the sea.

Switzerland has about 1500 lakes and countless streams and rivers. Big rivers such as the **Rhine**, the Rhone and the Inn rise here. A large part of the fresh water is stored in glaciers, lakes and groundwater. That is why Switzerland is called the **water tower of Europe**.

In Swiss waters live fish such as **whitefish**, brown trout, pike, perch and grayling.
