Added to these are many smaller animals such as freshwater shrimps, water snails, dragonfly larvae and caddisfly larvae. Mammals such as the beaver and birds such as the great crested grebe or the kingfisher also depend on fresh water. Many insects spend their youth as larvae in the water and only live on land as adults.

The body of a freshwater fish is saltier than the water around it. That is why water constantly seeps into its body through the skin and gills, which is called **osmosis**. The fish therefore hardly drinks and passes a lot of very dilute urine. Sea fish have the opposite problem, which is why most fish can live in only one of the two kinds of water.

Fresh water is scarce and valuable, also as drinking water for people. Pollution from fertiliser, waste water and microplastics harms the animals. Straightened rivers and dams destroy spawning grounds, and warmer water troubles cold-loving fish such as the grayling. In Switzerland, many streams and rivers are therefore being **restored to a natural state**, which means rebuilt to be close to nature.

begriffe.erklaerung: Water with very little dissolved salt, for example in rivers and lakes.
A mixture of fresh water and seawater, for example at river mouths.
Water moves through a thin skin from the side with less salt to the side with more salt.
A built-up waterway is made more natural again.

gewusst: Salmon and eels can change between fresh water and the sea because their bodies can adjust.
Most of the Earth’s fresh water is locked up in the ice of Antarctica and Greenland.
The water from many Swiss taps is so clean that it can be drunk straight from springs and groundwater without treatment.

teile.einleitung: The common earthworm, in German the Tauwurm or “dew worm”, is one of the most common large earthworms in Switzerland and in the whole of Europe. It can grow up to about 30 centimetres long and digs deep, vertical tunnels into the soil. At night it comes up to the surface to pull leaves into its burrow.
wichtigste: The common earthworm (Lumbricus terrestris) is a large species of earthworm.
Fully grown, it reaches up to about 30 centimetres long.
It digs vertical burrows that can reach two metres and deeper into the soil.
It has its German name because it comes up to the surface on damp, dewy nights.
It eats dead leaves and turns them into fertile humus.
Common earthworms are hermaphrodites, and each animal is male and female at the same time.

abschnitte.text: The common earthworm has a long, round body of over a hundred **segments**. The front end is reddish brown and strong, the rear end flatter and lighter. In adult worms you can see a thick, light ring, the **girdle** or clitellum. It has no eyes, ears or lungs, and breathes through its moist skin.

Common earthworms dig vertical **living burrows** that often reach two to three metres deep. In them they live for many years in the same place. At night they stretch the front of the body out of the burrow and pull leaves into it, while the rear end stays anchored in the burrow. In the morning you often see small piles of leaves and small piles of droppings over the burrow entrances on meadows.

The common earthworm eats dead leaves and soil with plant remains. Its droppings are especially nutrient-rich **humus**, which makes the soil fertile. Through its tunnels, air and rainwater get deep into the soil, and plant roots grow more easily. Farmers and gardeners are therefore glad to see many earthworms.

Common earthworms are **hermaphrodites**, but they still need a partner. On warm, damp nights two worms lie side by side at the surface and exchange seed. After that the girdle forms a slimy sheath from which a small **cocoon** with an egg arises. After a few weeks a tiny young worm hatches from it.

Common earthworms are eaten by blackbirds, hedgehogs, badgers, foxes and moles. The mole even lays in stores by paralysing worms with a bite and keeping them in its burrow. Anglers use common earthworms as **bait** for fish. When a worm is cut in two, by the way, two worms do not result, and usually at most the front part survives.

begriffe.erklaerung: A worm that lives in the soil and loosens and fertilises the earth.
A living thing that has both male and female sex organs.
A thickened ring in adult earthworms from which the cocoon arises.
A protective sheath in which an egg develops.

gewusst: Charles Darwin wrote his last book in 1881 about earthworms and showed how over decades they turn over whole layers of soil.
Under a meadow, several hundred earthworms can live per square metre.
A common earthworm can live for several years.

teile.einleitung: Partial migrants are bird species in which some of the animals fly south in autumn, while the others stay in their breeding area. Typical partial migrants in Switzerland are the blackbird, the robin and the chaffinch. Which bird goes and which stays depends on its genes, its age, its sex and the weather.
wichtigste: Partial migrants are birds of which some migrate and some stay.
Well-known partial migrants are the blackbird, robin, chaffinch, starling and blackcap.
Often it is rather the females and young birds that leave, while older males stay.
Partial migrants stand between the resident birds and the migratory birds.
Thanks to milder winters, more birds now stay in Switzerland over winter.
The Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach uses rings and transmitters to study how birds migrate.

abschnitte.text: In a **partial migrant**, not all birds of a species behave the same way. Some leave the breeding area in autumn and spend the winter in the south, for example in southern France, Spain or North Africa. The others stay there all winter. Partial migrants are therefore an in-between form between **resident birds** and **migratory birds**.

abschnitte.titel: Resident birds, migratory birds and wanderers
abschnitte.text: **Resident birds** such as the house sparrow, woodpeckers and nuthatches stay in their area all year round. **Migratory birds** such as the swift, barn swallow and cuckoo leave Switzerland every autumn and fly as far as Africa. Wandering birds only roam short distances in winter, depending on where they find food. In many species the transitions are gradual.

Whether a bird migrates is partly fixed in its **genes**. Age, sex and food supply also play a part. Often young birds and females are the ones to leave, while experienced males stay to take the best territories in spring. The researcher Carl Linnaeus therefore called the chaffinch the “bachelor”, because in Sweden it was mainly males that stayed behind in winter.

In winter you often see robins, blackbirds and chaffinches in Switzerland, but they are not always the same birds as in summer. Some native birds have left, while **winter visitors** from Scandinavia or eastern Europe have arrived. A robin at the bird table can therefore come from Sweden. We know this thanks to **ringing**: birds are given a small ring with a number on the leg.

Because winters are getting milder, more birds now stay in their breeding area. In the **blackcap** a new migration route has even developed: many animals from central Europe no longer spend the winter in Spain but in Great Britain. Partial migrants can adapt to changes faster than pure migratory birds. The **Swiss Ornithological Institute in Sempach** in the canton of Lucerne has been watching such changes for many decades.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird species in which only some of the animals leave in winter.
A bird that stays in the same area all year round.
A bird that travels back and forth every year between its breeding area and its winter quarters.
Marking birds with a numbered leg ring in order to study their routes.

gewusst: The scientific name of the chaffinch, Fringilla coelebs, means “unmarried finch”, because in winter often only the males stay in the north.
Blackbirds used to be regarded as shy woodland birds and only became town dwellers in the 19th century, and in towns they often no longer migrate at all.
Whether a young blackcap flies south-west or north-west is fixed in its genes.

teile.einleitung: The Sri Lankan elephant is a subspecies of the Asian elephant that lives on the island of Sri Lanka in the Indian Ocean. It is the largest subspecies of the Asian elephant. For the people of Sri Lanka it is an important symbol and takes part in many festivals.
wichtigste: The Sri Lankan elephant lives only on the island of Sri Lanka, south of India.
It is the largest subspecies of the Asian elephant.
Typical features are lighter, pink-spotted patches on the ears, face and trunk.
Only very few bulls have large tusks.
About 6000 wild elephants live in Sri Lanka (count of 2011).
The subspecies is seriously endangered, mainly because of the loss of its habitat.
At the Esala Perahera festival in Kandy, decorated elephants walk through the city.

abschnitte.text: Sri Lankan elephants have dark skin with light, pink patches without **pigment** on the ears, forehead, trunk and belly. Bulls can reach a shoulder height of up to three metres and weigh several tonnes. Like all Asian elephants, they have smaller ears than African elephants and an arched back. It is especially striking that only a small share of the bulls have real **tusks**.

The elephants live in forests, grasslands and scrubland in the lowlands of Sri Lanka, mostly in the drier north and east. Well-known protected areas are **Yala National Park** and Minneriya National Park. They need a lot of water and like to stay near lakes and reservoirs. A grown elephant eats well over 100 kilograms of grass, leaves, bark and fruit every day.

Females and young live in family groups led by an experienced **matriarch**. Adult bulls usually wander alone or in small bachelor groups. In the dry season, several hundred elephants often gather on the shore of a large reservoir in Minneriya National Park. This event is called “The Gathering” and is regarded as one of the largest gatherings of elephants in Asia.

Elephants have played an important part in the culture of Sri Lanka for over 2000 years. At the Buddhist festival **Esala Perahera** in Kandy, splendidly decorated elephants carry a casket with a sacred relic through the streets every year. At the Pinnawala Elephant Orphanage, founded in 1975, orphaned young elephants are raised. Tamed elephants were also used in the past for work in the forest.

The greatest danger is the loss of habitat, because forests are cleared for fields, villages and roads. This often leads to **conflicts** between people and elephants, which wander into fields and eat the crops. Every year hundreds of elephants and also many people die in Sri Lanka in such encounters. Protective fences, corridors between protected areas and education are meant to help people and elephants live together more peacefully.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group within a species that differs in its features and where it lives.
Lengthened front teeth of elephants, made of ivory.
The oldest and most experienced female, who leads an elephant herd.
A place where young animals without a mother are raised.

gewusst: Among Sri Lankan elephants only a few bulls have tusks, while among African elephants almost all of them do.
Elephants can communicate with one another over several kilometres using deep sounds that people cannot hear.
In relation to its area, Sri Lanka has one of the highest densities of elephants in Asia.

teile.einleitung: Spiracles, called “Stigmen” in German, are small breathing openings in the skin of insects, millipedes and other arthropods. Air flows through them into a fine system of tubes in the body. In this way these animals breathe without any lungs at all.
wichtigste: A spiracle (in German “Stigma”) is a breathing opening in insects and other arthropods.
Millipedes take in air through spiracles.
The spiracles are usually on the sides of the body.
From the spiracles, fine tubes called tracheae lead through the whole body.
Many insects can open and close their spiracles.
This way of breathing limits the size of insects.
In botany, “stigma” means something different, namely the stigma of a flower.

abschnitte.text: The German word Stigma comes from Greek and means dot or mark. In zoology it is the name for the tiny **breathing openings** in the outer covering of arthropods. They are also called breathing holes. In caterpillars they are easy to see as small dark dots on the side of each body ring.

Through the spiracles, air gets into a network of fine tubes, the **tracheae**. These branch out further and further until they reach right up to the cells. The oxygen therefore does not have to be carried by blood as it is in us. Many insects have small flaps or muscles with which they close the spiracles so that they do not dry out.

Insects usually have up to ten pairs of spiracles, two on the chest and up to eight on the abdomen. **Millipedes** and centipedes also breathe through spiracles and tracheae. Many spiders also have spiracles, which lead to book lungs or tracheae. Grasshoppers and bees pump with their abdomen to exchange the air faster.

Water insects have special tricks. The larvae of **mosquitoes** hang at the surface of the water and breathe through a breathing tube at the rear end. The great diving beetle takes an air bubble under its wing cases with it when it dives. In this way air reaches its spiracles even when it is under water.

Because oxygen travels only slowly through the tracheae, this kind of breathing works well only in small animals. About 300 million years ago, in the **Carboniferous**, the air contained more oxygen than today. At that time there lived giant dragonflies with a wingspan of over 60 centimetres. Today such giants are no longer possible.

In botany the sticky tip of the pistil of a flower is also called a stigma, in German **Narbe**. Pollen grains stick there. In many insects there is also a dark mark on the wing that is likewise called a stigma. Which meaning is intended can be told from the context.

begriffe.erklaerung: Fine, branching windpipes in the body of insects and millipedes.
Animals with a hard outer skeleton and jointed legs, for example insects, spiders and crustaceans.
The topmost, sticky part of the pistil of a flower, which catches the pollen.

gewusst: Insects have no blood that carries oxygen, and the air reaches the cells directly through the spiracles.
Because of the higher oxygen content of the air, there were dragonflies as big as crows about 300 million years ago.

teile.einleitung: Pure white cats with blue eyes are strikingly often deaf. The reason lies in their genes: the inherited trait that causes the white fur and the blue eyes often also disturbs development in the inner ear. The naturalist Charles Darwin already described this odd connection.
wichtigste: Pure white cats with blue eyes are deaf more often than other cats.
The gene for white fur and blue eyes is often linked to faulty development of the cochlea.
Depending on the study, about two thirds or more of white cats with two blue eyes are deaf.
If a white cat has only one blue eye, often only the ear on that side is deaf.
The deafness develops in the first weeks of life and cannot be cured.
Deaf cats can still lead a good life, best indoors or in a secured garden.

abschnitte.text: Many pure white cats carry a certain inherited trait that experts call **dominant white**. It prevents the pigment cells, the **melanocytes**, from spreading into the skin and fur. That is why the fur stays white, and often the pigment is also missing from the iris, so that the eyes look blue. Albino cats are something different: they have a different gene defect and usually reddish or very pale eyes.

The body needs pigment cells not only for colour but also in the inner ear. In the **cochlea** they help to make a special fluid that is needed for hearing. If they are missing, the fine **hearing cells** die in the first weeks of life. The kitten is born with apparently normal ears, but soon becomes deaf.

In white cats with two blue eyes the majority are deaf, depending on the study about two thirds or more. If the cat has one blue eye and one of another colour, clearly fewer are affected. Then often only the ear on the side of the blue eye is deaf. White cats without blue eyes can also be deaf, but much more rarely.

A cat that is deaf on one side behaves almost normally, so you often do not notice. Completely deaf cats do not react to calling, clapping or the vacuum cleaner, but they sense vibrations. Vets can measure hearing with a painless **hearing test** that records the brain waves in response to clicking sounds. Responsible breeders test white cats before they carry on breeding with them.

Deaf cats are normal, playful animals and do not suffer from their deafness. Outdoors, however, they are in danger, because they cannot hear cars or dogs. You communicate with them through **hand signals**, light or tapping on the floor. If you do not want to startle a deaf cat, it is best to approach it in such a way that it can see you.

begriffe.erklaerung: A section of the genetic material that controls a certain trait.
A snail-shaped part of the inner ear in which sound is turned into nerve signals.
Cells that make the pigment for skin, hair and eyes.
Unable to hear, or hardly able to hear.

gewusst: As early as 1859, in his famous book on the origin of species, Charles Darwin mentioned that white cats with blue eyes are usually deaf.
A similar connection between white colour and deafness also occurs in dogs such as the Dalmatian.
Many deaf cats miaow especially loudly, because they cannot hear their own voice.

teile.einleitung: A stampede is a wild, panicked flight of a whole herd of animals. When a herd of bison, cattle or wildebeest suddenly runs off in panic, the ground can shake. Weaker animals are often trampled in the process.
wichtigste: A stampede is a mass flight of a herd in panic.
When a herd of bison runs off in panic, it is called a stampede.
The triggers are often predators, thunderstorms, fire or loud noises.
The word comes from the Spanish “estampida” and means roughly a stamping or a bang.
Bison can reach over 50 kilometres per hour when fleeing.
In the Wild West, cowboys feared stampedes of their herds of cattle.
For crowds of people, too, the word stampede is sometimes used, meaning a mass panic.

abschnitte.text: A **stampede** happens when many herd animals take fright at the same time and run blindly in one direction. One animal runs off, the others follow without knowing what they are fleeing from. This behaviour is called the **herd instinct**. In the crowd each single animal is better protected from predators, but in a panic the herd itself can become dangerous.

Typical triggers are predators such as wolves or lions that attack a herd. Thunder, lightning, prairie fires or a sudden bang can also throw animals into a panic. In the past, even the rattle of a pan in the cowboys’ camp was sometimes enough. Herd animals are **prey animals** and would rather react too early than too late to danger.

In the past, huge herds of **American bison** roamed across the prairies of North America. Bison weigh up to a tonne, but can still run faster than 50 kilometres per hour. Some Indigenous peoples deliberately drove herds of bison over cliffs in order to hunt them. A well-known place for this is Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump in Canada, today a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

In East Africa, over a million **wildebeest** migrate every year together with zebras through the Serengeti and the Masai Mara. When they cross rivers such as the Mara, the animals crowd on to the bank and often plunge into the water in panic. Crocodiles lie in wait there, and in the rush many animals drown or are injured. These river crossings are among the most impressive natural spectacles in the world.

In the 19th century, cowboys drove large **herds of cattle** for hundreds of kilometres to the railway stations. A stampede at night was feared, because animals and riders could be killed or hurt. The cowboys therefore often sang softly to the cattle to calm them. Today the big rodeo festival, the Calgary Stampede in Canada, which has existed since 1912, recalls that time.

begriffe.erklaerung: The tendency of herd animals to do what the others do.
An animal that saves itself from danger mainly by running away.
A wide grassland in North America.
When a large crowd becomes afraid and flees out of control.

gewusst: A running herd of bison can be heard and felt as a rumble from a long way off.
Despite their weight, bison are good jumpers and swimmers.
The Calgary Stampede attracts over a million visitors every year.

teile.einleitung: The minotaur beetle is a shiny black dung beetle whose male carries three horns on its pronotum. With them it looks like a little armoured bull. It lives mainly in sandy areas and collects droppings from rabbits and sheep.
wichtigste: The minotaur beetle belongs to the dung beetle family.
It is about 1.5 to 2 centimetres long and shiny black.
The male typically carries three horns on its pronotum.
The horns are probably used for fights with other males.
Minotaur beetles and their larvae often feed on the droppings of rabbits and sheep.
It likes best to live on sandy heaths and pastures.
Male and female work together to build the brood tunnel.

abschnitte.text: The minotaur beetle grows to about 14 to 20 millimetres long and is black and shiny. The male has three horns on the **pronotum**. Two long horns point forwards and reach beyond the head, with a short third horn between them. The females have only small bumps. Its scientific name is Typhaeus typhoeus.

The minotaur beetle is found in western and central Europe. It needs loose, **sandy soil** in which it can dig well. Typical places are heaths, dunes, sandy pastures and woodland edges. Many rabbits or sheep often live there, and it needs their droppings.

Minotaur beetles are **dung feeders**. They collect mainly the small, dry droppings of rabbits and sheep. They take these underground, where they are food for the larvae. In this way they help to break down dung and to fertilise the soil.

abschnitte.titel: Caring for the young as a pair
abschnitte.text: Male and female work together, which is rare among beetles. The female digs a vertical **brood tunnel**, which can be over a metre deep. The male carries the soil out and fetches droppings. At the end of the tunnel the droppings are pressed into a sort of dung sausage, on which the female lays an egg. The **larva** eats the store and pupates in the soil.

With his horns the male defends the brood tunnel against other males. When two males fight, they try to push each other out of the tunnel. Bigger males with longer horns usually have better chances. Such **horns** in beetles often have exactly this purpose.

abschnitte.titel: Active in the winter half of the year
abschnitte.text: Unlike many other beetles, the minotaur beetle is active mainly in the cool season. It can be seen from autumn until spring, sometimes even on mild winter days. In summer it rests deep in the soil. Because heaths and pastures with rabbits are becoming rarer, it has become rare in many places.

begriffe.erklaerung: A beetle family whose members feed on the droppings of larger animals.
The armoured part between a beetle’s head and its wing cases.
The young stage of an insect, which still looks quite different from the grown animal.
Everything that parent animals do to look after and protect their offspring.

gewusst: The brood tunnel of a minotaur beetle can reach deeper than a child is tall.
In the minotaur beetle the males help with building the nest, which is only rarely the case in insects.

teile.einleitung: The tiger shark is a large shark from warm seas that has dark stripes like a big cat. It is regarded as one of the least fussy eaters in the sea and eats almost anything it finds. At several metres long, it is one of the largest predatory fish.
wichtigste: The tiger shark has stripes on its skin like a big cat.
Its scientific name is Galeocerdo cuvier.
It belongs to the order of ground sharks (Carcharhiniformes).
The tiger shark is the only living species of its genus.
It eats almost anything it finds.
It lives in tropical and subtropical seas all over the world.
Its snout is short, broad and blunt.

abschnitte.text: The tiger shark gets its name from the dark **cross stripes**, which can be seen best in young animals. In older animals they fade. Its snout is short, broad and blunt. Most adult tiger sharks are three to four metres long, and very large females grow to over five metres long and weigh several hundred kilograms.

Tiger sharks live in tropical and subtropical seas around the world, for example around Hawaii, Australia, in the Caribbean and in the Indian Ocean. They often stay near the coast, in lagoons, river mouths and at coral reefs. At night they often come into shallow water, and by day they tend to swim in deeper water. Some animals cover thousands of kilometres on their migrations.

The tiger shark is not fussy and eats almost anything it finds. Its menu includes fish, other sharks, sea turtles, seabirds, sea snakes, seals and carrion. With its serrated, cockscomb-shaped **teeth** it can even crack turtle shells. In the stomachs of tiger sharks, people have found number plates, plastic and other rubbish.

The tiger shark was first described scientifically in 1822 as **Squalus cuvier**, and it bears its species name in honour of the naturalist Georges Cuvier. The genus Galeocerdo was set up by Johannes Müller and Jakob Henle in 1837. The name is put together from the Greek words for “shark” and “fox”. In the past it was counted among the requiem sharks, but the Catalog of Fishes and FishBase now place it in a family of its own, the **Galeocerdonidae**.

Unlike many other sharks, tiger sharks do not lay eggs in the water. The young develop in eggs inside the mother and hatch there before they are born alive. A litter can consist of 10 to 80 young. The newborns are about half a metre long and are on their own at once.

The tiger shark is one of the few sharks that can also be dangerous to people, and after the great white shark it causes the most bite accidents. Such accidents are very rare, though. The danger coming from people is much greater, because tiger sharks are caught for their fins, meat and liver. The International Union for Conservation of Nature classes the tiger shark as **near threatened**.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large order of sharks that also includes hammerhead sharks and catsharks, for example.
The flesh of dead animals.
A group of very closely related species.
Sense organs on the head of sharks with which they detect weak electric fields.

gewusst: With their sense organs, tiger sharks can detect the weak electric signals of animals hidden in the sand.
Because tiger sharks eat so many different things, they are sometimes called the “rubbish bins of the sea”.
A female tiger shark can give birth to as many as 80 young at one time.

teile.einleitung: The death's-head hawkmoth is a large night-flying moth with a yellow marking on its back that looks like a skull. It is the largest hawkmoth in Europe and flies as a migrant from Africa and southern Europe as far as Switzerland. It can also squeak and steals honey from beehives.
wichtigste: The death's-head hawkmoth belongs to the hawkmoth family (Sphingidae).
Its scientific name is Acherontia atropos.
Carl Linnaeus first described it in 1758, at that time under the genus name Sphinx.
It has a skull-like yellow marking on the thorax.
It is the largest hawkmoth in Europe.
Females reach a wingspan of about 10 to 12 cm.
It is a migrant moth that flies to us from the south.

abschnitte.text: On its thorax the moth has a yellow marking that reminds people of a **skull**. The forewings are marbled dark brown, and the hind wings are ochre yellow with two dark bands. Females reach a wingspan of about 10 to 12 centimetres, rarely up to 13 centimetres, and weigh about 3 to 8 grams. The antennae are black with a white tip.

Carl Linnaeus described the moth in 1758 and at first placed it in the genus **Sphinx**. The present genus name Acherontia goes back to the Acheron, a river of the Greek underworld. The species name recalls **Atropos**, one of the three Fates of Greek legend, who cuts the thread of life. Because of its appearance, the moth was once regarded as a bringer of bad luck.

The death's-head hawkmoth lives mainly in Africa and around the Mediterranean. In early summer some moths fly as **migrants** over the Alps to central Europe and Switzerland. Here they lay eggs, from which a new generation hatches in late summer. The pupae usually do not survive the cold winter here.

The caterpillar feeds mainly on potatoes, tomatoes and other **nightshades**. It grows to about 12 centimetres long and is mostly yellow-green with blue slanting stripes. At the rear end it has a curved horn, like many hawkmoth caterpillars. To turn into a pupa it digs deep into the soil.

The death's-head hawkmoth has a short, strong proboscis and breaks into **beehives** at night to drink honey. It smells similar to the bees and is therefore often not attacked. If it is disturbed, it can make a high squeak by pressing air through its proboscis. The caterpillar and the pupa can also make sounds.

begriffe.erklaerung: A family of strong, fast-flying night moths.
A butterfly or moth that flies over long distances to other regions every year.
The three goddesses of destiny in Greek legend.
A plant family that includes the potato, tomato and pepper.

gewusst: The death's-head hawkmoth is one of the few butterflies and moths that can make audible sounds.
There are three species of death's-head hawkmoth worldwide, called Acherontia atropos, Acherontia lachesis and Acherontia styx.
In the past people were afraid of the moth, because they took the skull on its back for an evil sign.

teile.einleitung: Gestation is the name for the time in which a female mammal carries young in her body. In humans we call this pregnancy. How long it lasts differs very much from one animal species to another, from just under two weeks to almost two years.
wichtigste: Gestation is the time from fertilisation to birth in animals.
The gestation of a female dog lasts about 63 days.
Large animals usually carry their young longer than small ones.
Elephants carry their young for almost two years.
Cows carry their calf for about nine months.
In the roe deer there is a delay before the embryo develops, which lengthens the gestation.
Vets can detect a pregnancy with ultrasound.

abschnitte.text: **Gestation** begins with the fertilisation of an egg cell and ends with birth. During this time the young one grows in the womb and is supplied with nutrients through the **placenta**. The length of time is also called the gestation period. In humans we do not speak of gestation but of pregnancy.

A female dog is pregnant for about 63 days, and a cat for about the same time. A rabbit gives birth to its young after only about a month, and a mouse even after about three weeks. A cow carries her calf for about nine months, and a mare her foal for about eleven months. At about 22 months, the African elephant holds the record among land animals.

Large animals are usually pregnant longer than small ones. For pigs, farmers remember the rule “three months, three weeks and three days”. Marsupials such as kangaroos have a very short gestation, and the young go on growing afterwards in the **pouch**. The young of horses or giraffes can walk soon after birth, but puppies and kittens are born blind and helpless.

In some animals such as the roe deer, the badger or the bear, the embryo takes a pause. This is called **delayed implantation**. Roe deer mate in high summer, but the embryo only really goes on developing from winter. That is how the fawns are born in May or June, when there is enough food.

Whether an animal is pregnant can be found out by the vet using ultrasound or by feeling the belly. Pregnant animals need more and special food, rest and a sheltered place for the birth. There are special words for giving birth: a cow **calves**, a mare foals, a sow farrows, and a female dog whelps. Anyone who does not want young animals can have their pet neutered.

begriffe.erklaerung: The length of the gestation.
An organ in the womb through which the young one receives food and oxygen.
A pause in the development of the embryo that makes the gestation longer.
All the young that an animal brings into the world at one birth.

gewusst: Some opossums in America are pregnant for only about two weeks.
A baby elephant weighs about 100 kilograms at birth.
Depending on the breed, a female dog can have more than ten puppies in one litter.

teile.einleitung: The tapetum lucidum is a mirror-like layer behind the retina in the eyes of many animals. It throws the incoming light back so that the sense cells can use it a second time. That is why cats can still see well in very little light, and their eyes glow in the dark when you shine a light on them.
wichtigste: Tapetum lucidum is Latin and means “shining carpet”.
The layer lies behind the retina and works like a mirror.
It strengthens the light by sending leftover light through the retina a second time.
Cats, jaguars, dogs, deer and many other animals have a tapetum lucidum.
Humans do not have one, which is why we see badly in the dark.
The glow of animal eyes in the light of headlamps comes from this layer.

abschnitte.text: The **tapetum lucidum** is a thin layer of tissue in the eye that reflects light. It usually lies directly behind the **retina**, where the light-sensitive sense cells sit. In cats it consists of tiny crystals, and in other animals of fibres or cells with reflecting substances. The name means roughly “shining carpet” in English.

Light falls through the pupil into the eye and hits the retina. Part of it is not caught by the sense cells and would be lost. The tapetum throws this **leftover light** back so that it can hit the sense cells a second time. In this way the eye uses much more of the light that is available, but the picture is a little less sharp as a result.

It is especially well developed in animals that hunt at dusk or at night, such as **cats**, jaguars and foxes. Dogs, horses, cattle, deer, crocodiles and many sharks and fish also have one. Most monkeys, pigs and humans do not have a tapetum lucidum. Cats need only a small fraction of the light that a human needs to see.

When a car headlamp or a torch shines on an animal at night, its eyes light up brightly. This is called **eyeshine**. Depending on the species of animal, it shimmers green, yellow, blue or reddish. Foresters and gamekeepers can in this way tell in the dark whether a deer, a fox or a cat is sitting in the bushes.

The reflectors on a bicycle and the reflective studs at the roadside are called **cat’s eyes**, after the animals. In 1934 the Englishman Percy Shaw invented road reflectors that he called “Cat’s Eyes”. They throw the light of the headlamps back to the driver. The red glow of the eyes in flash photos of people, on the other hand, has nothing to do with a tapetum, and comes from the retina, which is well supplied with blood.

begriffe.erklaerung: The inner layer of the eye with sense cells that turn light into nerve signals.
To throw light back like a mirror.
The black opening in the middle of the eye through which light falls in.
A part on a bicycle or on the road that throws light back, also called a cat’s eye.

gewusst: In photos with flash, cats’ eyes often glow green or yellow, while human eyes glow red.
Some spiders such as wolf spiders also have reflecting eyes that sparkle in torchlight.
Cattle have a tapetum that often shimmers bluish to greenish in the light.

teile.einleitung: Theobromine is a natural substance from the cocoa bean and is therefore found in chocolate. For people it is harmless in small amounts and has a mildly stimulating effect. For cats and dogs, however, theobromine is poisonous.
wichtigste: Theobromine is found mainly in the cocoa bean.
Chocolate is dangerous for cats, because theobromine is poisonous to them.
Chocolate is poisonous to dogs as well.
Animals such as dogs and cats break down theobromine only very slowly.
Dark chocolate contains much more theobromine than milk chocolate.
Theobromine is a close relative of caffeine.
If poisoning is suspected, the animal must go to the vet at once.

abschnitte.text: Theobromine is a bitter substance from the group of **alkaloids**. Its name comes from the cacao tree, which is called Theobroma cacao in science. Theobroma is Greek and means “food of the gods”. Chemically, theobromine is very similar to caffeine, but it is weaker in its effect.

Most theobromine is in the seeds of the cacao tree, the **cocoa beans**. That is why cocoa powder and dark chocolate contain especially much of it. Milk chocolate contains clearly less, and white chocolate almost none, because it is made only of cocoa butter. Small amounts are also found in tea and in the kola nut.

People break down theobromine in a few hours. In cats and dogs it takes much longer, so that the substance builds up in the body and acts as a **poison**. Typical signs of poisoning are vomiting, diarrhoea, restlessness, heavy panting, a fast heartbeat and, in the worst case, fits. Even a bar of dark chocolate can be life-threatening for a small dog.

abschnitte.titel: What to do in an emergency
abschnitte.text: If a pet has eaten chocolate, you should call the **vet** straight away. It is important to know what kind and how much the animal has eaten. Often the vet can make the animal vomit or give it activated charcoal, which binds the poison. That is why the rule is: always keep chocolate tightly closed and out of reach of animals.

Theobromine was discovered in cocoa beans in 1841 by the Russian chemist Alexander Voskresensky. In people it has a mildly stimulating effect, widens the blood vessels and stimulates the kidneys. In Switzerland people eat on average about ten kilograms of chocolate per person per year (as of the 2020s). For people, normal amounts of chocolate are no problem because of the theobromine.

begriffe.erklaerung: A natural, often bitter substance from plants that can have a strong effect in the body.
The seed of the cacao tree from which chocolate is made.
Harm in the body caused by a poisonous substance.
A stimulating substance that is found in coffee, for example.

gewusst: Cats cannot taste sweetness and therefore eat chocolate less often than dogs.
The darker the chocolate, the more dangerous it is for dogs and cats.
Cocoa shells, which are sometimes used as garden mulch, also contain theobromine.

teile.einleitung: The golden eagle is a mighty bird of prey that in Switzerland lives mainly in the Alps. With its broad wings it circles high above peaks and valleys and looks out for marmots and mountain hares. It is regarded as the king of the skies and is one of the best-known wild animals of the mountains.
wichtigste: The golden eagle is one of the largest birds of prey in the Alps, and only the bearded vulture has a bigger wingspan.
Its wingspan is about 1.9 to 2.3 metres.
The females are larger and heavier than the males.
Adult golden eagles usually stay in the same territory all year round.
Young golden eagles have striking white patches on their wings and tail.
It hunts mainly marmots, mountain hares and ptarmigans, but occasionally also eats carrion.
About 300 pairs breed in Switzerland (estimate from around 2020).

abschnitte.text: The golden eagle is dark brown with a golden-brown neck, which is why it is called the Golden Eagle in English. Its legs are **feathered** down to the toes, which sets it apart from the white-tailed eagle, with its bare legs. The females are clearly larger than the males and weigh up to about six and a half kilograms. Young golden eagles can be recognised by the large **white patches** on the wings and tail, which disappear over the years.

In Switzerland the golden eagle lives almost only in the **Alps**, mostly between the tree line and the peaks. A pair lives in a territory of often 50 to 100 square kilometres and stays there all year round. They defend their area against strange eagles with flying displays. Golden eagles are therefore resident birds and do not move away in winter.

The golden eagle uses the **thermals**, that is, warm rising air, and glides for a long time without a wingbeat over the slopes. When it spots prey, it swoops down in a dive and seizes it with its strong talons. Its most important prey in the Alps is the marmot, and besides that it hunts mountain hares, ptarmigans, foxes and young chamois. In winter it occasionally also eats carrion, for example from animals that have died in avalanches.

The nest is called an **eyrie** and consists mainly of branches and twigs, mostly on a rock face. A pair often uses its eyrie again and again for many years and extends it every year. The female usually lays one or two eggs and sits on them for about six weeks, while the male often brings her food. The young leave the nest after about ten to eleven weeks and are then still looked after by their parents for a few more weeks.

In the past the golden eagle was hunted as a supposed sheep thief and had become rare in Switzerland. Since it has been **protected**, its numbers have recovered, and today the territories in the Swiss Alps are largely occupied. Among the greatest dangers today are collisions with **power lines** and disturbance by people, for example by climbers, drones or paragliders near the eyrie. Lead poisoning from leftover ammunition in carrion is also a problem.

begriffe.erklaerung: A bird with strong talons and a hooked beak that hunts other animals.
The large nest of birds of prey, mostly made of branches.
Rising warm air that birds use to climb without flapping their wings.
An area that an animal lives in and defends against others of its kind.

gewusst: A golden eagle can spot a marmot from over a kilometre away.
In a dive, the golden eagle reaches very high speeds of well over 150 kilometres per hour.
Often, of two chicks in the eyrie only the older one survives, because it pushes the younger one out.

teile.einleitung: The Tapanuli orangutan is a species of great ape that lives only in a small mountain forest on the island of Sumatra in Indonesia. It was only described as a species of its own in 2017, as the third species of orangutan alongside the Bornean and the Sumatran orangutan. With fewer than 800 animals, it is the rarest great ape in the world.
wichtigste: The Tapanuli orangutan (Pongo tapanuliensis) was described as a species of its own in 2017.
It lives only in the Batang Toru forest in the north of Sumatra.
There are fewer than 800 animals left.
That makes it the rarest species of great ape, and it is critically endangered.
It has curlier, cinnamon-coloured fur and a smaller skull than other orangutans.
It is threatened by logging, roads, mining and a hydroelectric power station.

abschnitte.titel: A new species of great ape
abschnitte.text: In 2017, researchers found that the orangutans south of Lake Toba on Sumatra are a **species of their own**. To do this they compared the genetic material of many animals as well as the skull of a male. It was the first newly described **species of great ape** for almost 90 years. It is named after the region of Tapanuli in the province of North Sumatra.

The Tapanuli orangutan has **curlier, cinnamon-coloured fur** than its relatives. Its skull and teeth are somewhat smaller and shaped differently. Adult males have flat **cheek pads** with downy hair and a striking beard. Their loud calls, with which they communicate over long distances, also sound different.

The animals live in the **Batang Toru forest**, a hilly mountain rainforest of only about 1000 square kilometres. That is smaller than the area of the canton of Lucerne. Orangutans spend almost their whole life in the treetops and build themselves a **sleeping nest** of branches every night. They eat mainly fruit, and also leaves, bark and insects.

Female orangutans have a young one only about every eight to nine years. The child stays with the mother for that long and learns which fruits are edible and how to build nests. That is the longest gap between two births of any mammal. That is why the populations can only recover very slowly after losses.

Even a few animals killed per year can bring the species to the edge of extinction. Threats are logging, plantations, a gold mine and above all a large **hydroelectric power station** that is being built in the middle of its habitat. The International Union for Conservation of Nature, IUCN, classes the species as **critically endangered**. Conservation organisations call for the last pieces of forest to be connected and protected for good.

begriffe.erklaerung: A group of large apes without a tail: orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos.
Broad pads on the face of adult male orangutans.
The blueprint of a living thing in every cell, also called DNA.
The International Union for Conservation of Nature, which publishes the Red Lists of threatened species; its seat is in Gland in the canton of Vaud.

gewusst: The word “orangutan” comes from Malay and means “person of the forest”.
According to genetic studies, the Tapanuli orangutan is more closely related to the Bornean orangutan than to the Sumatran orangutan, although it lives on Sumatra.
That orangutans live on Sumatra south of Lake Toba only became known to science in the 1990s.

teile.einleitung: Butterflies are the moths and butterflies that fly by day and are often splendidly coloured. They can usually be recognised by their antennae, which have a small thickening at the end. They include well-known species such as the peacock butterfly, the brimstone and the swallowtail.
wichtigste: Most well-known butterflies are active by day.
The antennae of butterflies often have a small thickening at the end like a club.
At rest, butterflies usually fold their wings together upright over the back.
There are almost 20 000 species worldwide, and about 200 in Switzerland.
Butterflies develop from the egg through the caterpillar and the pupa to the adult butterfly.
Many butterflies are endangered because flower-rich meadows are disappearing.

abschnitte.text: Butterflies are a group of **lepidopterans** that are out and about in sunshine. Most species of lepidopteran are in fact moths, but butterflies are the best known, because we see them. Typical are the **club-shaped antennae**, which are thickened at the end. Many moths, by contrast, have thread-like or feathery antennae.

The wings of butterflies are covered with tiny **scales** arranged like roof tiles. These produce the colours, some through pigments, others through the bending of light, which produces shimmering blues. Anyone who touches a butterfly often has fine dust on their fingers afterwards, which is rubbed-off scales. The upper side is often colourful, while the underside is often plain for camouflage.

Butterflies go through a complete **metamorphosis**. A caterpillar hatches from the egg, which eats and grows and moults several times. Then it changes into a pupa, which in butterflies often hangs freely from a stem. Finally the finished butterfly hatches from the pupa, and with its **proboscis** it sucks nectar from flowers.

The common butterflies of Switzerland include the peacock butterfly, the small tortoiseshell, the red admiral and the large white. The bright yellow **brimstone** often flies on the first warm days in February or March. The **swallowtail** is one of the largest and most beautiful butterflies in central Europe. In the Alps there are special species such as the Apollo butterfly and many ringlets.

Some butterflies are true migrants: the **painted lady** flies every year from North Africa across the Mediterranean and the Alps as far as central Europe. Many other species, however, have become rare. The reasons are intensive farming, fertiliser, pesticides and early mowing. Anyone who lets native flowers and a corner of nettles grow in the garden helps the butterflies.

begriffe.erklaerung: A lepidopteran that is active by day.
The change of an animal from a larva to the adult animal.
A long, coiling sucking tube with which butterflies drink nectar.
Tiny plates that cover the wings and give them their colour.

gewusst: Many butterflies taste with their feet: with sensory cells on their legs, they test whether a plant is suitable for their eggs.
Butterflies need the warmth of the sun to fly and warm up in the morning with their wings spread out.
On its migrations over several generations, the painted lady covers many thousands of kilometres.

teile.einleitung: The peacock butterfly is one of the best-known butterflies in Switzerland. On each of its four reddish-brown wings it has a big, colourful spot that looks like an eye. With these eyespots it can frighten enemies such as birds.
wichtigste: The peacock butterfly (Aglais io) is a butterfly from the family of brush-footed butterflies.
It has a pattern that looks like eyes, similar to the feathers of a peacock.
The eyespots are used to frighten enemies.
The caterpillar likes to eat nettles best.
The butterfly spends the winter as an adult animal, for example in cellars, sheds or tree holes.
It is found all over Switzerland, from the lowlands up into the mountains.

abschnitte.text: The peacock butterfly has a wingspan of about 5 to 6 centimetres. The upper side of the wings is bright **reddish brown**, each with a big eyespot in blue, yellow and black. The name recalls the shimmering eyes on the tail feathers of the **peacock**. The underside, by contrast, is almost black and looks like a withered leaf or tree bark.

When the butterfly is resting, it keeps its wings folded together and is well camouflaged. If a bird or a mouse comes near, it suddenly opens its wings and shows the **eyespots**. The enemy is startled, because it thinks that a big animal is looking at it. In addition the butterfly can make a **hissing noise** by rubbing its wings, which drives off mice, for example.

The female lays her eggs in large groups on the underside of **nettle leaves**. The black caterpillars with white dots and spines at first live together in a web. They eat almost only nettles, which many other animals cannot eat because of the stinging hairs. After a few weeks they pupate, and the finished butterfly hatches from the pupa.

Adult peacock butterflies suck **nectar** from flowers with their proboscis. Especially popular are buddleia, thistles, hemp agrimony and marjoram. In Switzerland there are one or two generations per year, depending on the altitude. The butterflies of the late-summer generation live especially long, because they survive the winter.

In autumn the peacock butterfly looks for a sheltered hiding place such as a cellar, an attic, a cave or a hollow tree. There it falls into a **winter torpor** and survives temperatures below zero. On the first warm days of spring it flies out again and soon lays eggs. A peacock butterfly can in this way live for almost a whole year, which is very long for a butterfly.

begriffe.erklaerung: A round, coloured pattern on the wings that looks like an eye.
A large family of butterflies that also includes the red admiral and the small tortoiseshell.
A state in which an animal stays almost motionless through the winter.
A fine net of silk threads that caterpillars build.

gewusst: The peacock butterfly can also make ultrasonic clicks with its wings, which probably confuse bats.
Anyone who leaves nettles standing in the garden creates a nursery for peacock butterflies.
Peacock butterflies spending the winter sometimes wake up in a warm flat in January and flutter about in confusion.

teile.einleitung: Squirrel monkeys are small, nimble monkeys from the rainforests of Central and South America. In German they are called Totenkopfaffen, or “skull monkeys”, because of their pale face with the black muzzle, which reminds people of a skull. They live in large groups and are almost always on the move.
wichtigste: Squirrel monkeys belong to the family Cebidae, the capuchin and squirrel monkey family.
The genus Saimiri is the only one in its subfamily Saimiriinae.
As New World monkeys, they have nostrils that point outwards to the side.
The German name comes from the black muzzle in the pale, mask-like face.
Their body is about 26 to 36 cm long, and the tail is even longer.
They use the tail as a balancing aid when climbing and leaping.
They live in large groups and eat insects and fruit.

abschnitte.text: Squirrel monkeys are small, and the head and body are only about 26 to 36 centimetres long. The tail is longer than the head and body together, but cannot grasp. Adults use it mainly as a **balancing aid** when climbing and leaping. The fur is olive grey on the back and often yellowish on the arms and legs, and the face is white with a black muzzle.

The German name comes from the pale, mask-like face with the black **muzzle**, which reminds people of a skull. In English it is called the “squirrel monkey”, because of its nimble movements. The genus name **Saimiri** comes from a language of the native peoples of South America and means roughly “little monkey”. Squirrel monkeys belong to the family of capuchin monkeys, and there they form the subfamily Saimiriinae as its only genus.

Squirrel monkeys live in the rainforests of the Amazon region, and one species is found in Costa Rica and Panama. As **New World monkeys** they have, like all the monkeys of the Americas, nostrils that point outwards to the side. Until 1984 all South American squirrel monkeys were regarded as one single, widespread species. Today they are divided into two groups, depending on the shape of the white patch above the eyes: in the Bolivian group it forms a round arch, and in the Sciureus group a pointed one.

Squirrel monkeys are active by day and very lively. They eat mainly **insects**, spiders and fruit, and sometimes also flowers, nectar and small vertebrates. They live in groups often of several dozen animals and communicate with many different calls. They often travel through the forest together with capuchin monkeys.

After a pregnancy of about five to six months, a female usually gives birth to a single young one. In the first weeks the young one clings to the mother's back. In some species other females of the group also help to carry it. In this way the young learn early how to find their way in the large **group**.

At the site of La Venta in Colombia, fossil relatives of the squirrel monkeys were found that are often called **Neosaimiri**. These finds are about 12 to 13 million years old. Today some species are threatened by the clearing of the rainforest and the animal trade. In many zoos in Europe you can watch squirrel monkeys in walk-through enclosures.

begriffe.erklaerung: Monkeys from Central and South America with nostrils that point to the side.
A group of very closely related species.
Petrified remains of living things from earlier times.
An animal that is out and about by day and sleeps at night.

gewusst: In relation to body size, squirrel monkeys have one of the largest brains of all monkeys.
Squirrel monkeys sometimes rub themselves with urine in order to leave scent trails.
A squirrel monkey usually weighs less than a kilogram, so roughly as much as a bag of flour.

teile.einleitung: Separation anxiety in dogs means that a dog shows strong stress behaviour as soon as it is left alone. Dogs are pack animals and are often very attached to their people. With patience and training, however, you can teach a dog to stay alone calmly.
wichtigste: Separation anxiety is strong stress behaviour when a dog is left alone.
Dogs are descended from the wolf and by nature live in groups.
Typical signs are barking, howling, scratching at doors and chewing things up.
Some dogs pant heavily or make a mess in the home out of stress.
Dogs that have never learned to be alone are especially often affected.
You practise staying alone slowly, in very small steps.
Punishment makes the fear worse and does not help.

abschnitte.text: In **separation anxiety** a dog panics when its main person goes away. This is not disobedience and not revenge either. The dog really feels threatened and helpless. Its body releases **stress hormones**, much as in a person who is very frightened.

Many dogs bark, howl or whine for a long time after their person has gone. Others scratch at the door, chew up cushions or shoes, or try to break out. Some pant, drool heavily or pace restlessly back and forth. Often the behaviour starts in the very first minutes. A **video camera** in the home can show what the dog really does.

Dogs are **social animals**, and their ancestors, the wolves, live in packs. A dog that was never alone as a puppy does not know this situation. Big changes can also trigger separation anxiety, for example a move, a new keeper or a stay in an animal shelter. After times when someone was always at home, some dogs also have trouble.

In training the dog learns that its person always comes back. At first you leave the room for only a few seconds and increase the time very slowly. What matters is that the dog stays calm. A fixed **retreat place** such as a basket and a chew toy help. Leaving and coming back should be as calm and unexciting as possible.

With strong fear, **vets** and dog trainers can help. They also check whether an illness lies behind the behaviour. In Switzerland there are vets with extra training in behavioural medicine for this. Sometimes a dog sitter or a dog day care centre is also a good solution until the training works.

begriffe.erklaerung: Behaviour that shows that an animal feels very uneasy or afraid.
The person to whom a dog is most strongly attached.
Slowly getting used to something that causes fear, in small steps.
An animal that by nature lives in a group.

gewusst: Dogs can tell from sounds such as the jingling of keys that their person is about to leave.
A dog with separation anxiety often waits right by the door until its person comes back.
Cats and parrots can also suffer from separation stress.

teile.einleitung: The tiger is the largest cat species in the world. With its orange coat and black stripes, it is perfectly camouflaged in the jungle. Today wild tigers live only in Asia, and they are badly endangered.
wichtigste: The tiger is the largest cat species in the world.
A large male tiger can weigh up to 300 kilograms.
Its coat is mostly orange with black stripes.
The stripes go right down to the skin.
Tigers sneak up quietly on their prey and surprise it.
They eat mainly deer and wild boar.
Wild tigers now live only in Asia and are badly endangered.

abschnitte.text: The tiger belongs to the family of **cats** and to the genus of big cats. Large males grow to about three metres long including the tail and weigh up to 300 kilograms, while females are smaller. The coat is mostly orange with black stripes, and the belly and throat are white. The stripes go right down to the skin, and every tiger has its own pattern, like a fingerprint.

Tigers live in rainforests, mangrove swamps, grasslands and the cold forests of eastern Russia. In the past they were found from Turkey to Indonesia. Today most wild tigers live in **India**, with others in Russia, Nepal, Bangladesh, Thailand, Malaysia and on Sumatra. Worldwide there are about 5500 wild tigers (estimate for 2023).

Tigers eat mainly the meat of deer and wild boar, and sometimes buffalo or monkeys. They hide in tall grass or bushes and creep up quietly on their prey. Then they surprise it with a short, powerful leap. On each front paw they have five retractable **claws**, and on the hind paws four.

Tigers are **loners** and are mostly out and about at dusk and at night. They mark their territory with scent marks and scratch marks on trees. Their roar can be heard several kilometres away. Unlike many cats, tigers love swimming and are very good at it.

About three months after mating, the tigress usually gives birth to two to four cubs. The cubs are blind at birth and weigh around a kilogram. The mother raises them alone and teaches them to hunt. At about two years old the young tigers become independent.

The tiger is badly endangered by **poaching**, the destruction of its habitat and a lack of prey animals. The subspecies on Bali and Java and the Caspian tiger have already died out. Thanks to protected areas, numbers in India and Nepal have been rising again for some years. In Switzerland you can watch Amur tigers at Zurich Zoo, for example.

begriffe.erklaerung: A large cat that can often roar, for example the lion, tiger or leopard.
The area that an animal regards as its own and defends.
The illegal hunting of protected animals.
An animal that lives alone most of the time.

gewusst: If you shaved a tiger's fur, you would still see the stripes on its skin.
Many prey animals such as deer see the orange of the tiger as green, which is why it is well camouflaged to them.
A tiger can eat more than 30 kilograms of meat in a single meal.
